paras: You run the support team at a travel company. Your director wants three people AWS AI Practitioner certified by spring, and you're one of them. You've used a chatbot. You've never trained a model, and you don't code.
So you buy a popular video course and a practice test from a well-reviewed website. Then, out of curiosity, you open the official exam guide.

The guide is dated April 30, 2026. It names Kiro, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Your video course never says any of those words. It spends twenty minutes on tools the guide no longer lists at all.
You haven't studied a single topic yet, and you've already found the first trap. Which of your sources is describing the exam you'll actually sit?
It's Tuesday, 4:40pm. Your director drops a message in the team channel: “Three of us get AWS AI Practitioner by spring. Company pays. You're on the list.”
You lead a support team at a travel company. You use a chatbot to draft replies. You have never trained a model, and the word “algorithm” makes you slightly nervous.
That evening you buy a top-rated video course. The instructor is confident and funny. By lesson three you're taking neat notes on a tool called PartyRock.

Then you open the official exam guide, just to check. Version 1.1, dated April 30, 2026. You search it for PartyRock. Nothing. You search for Kiro, a name the instructor never mentioned. There it is, in scope.
You close the laptop. Before you learn anything about AI, you need to know one thing. What does the exam you'll sit actually ask?

lab.setup: Here is a question in the style AWS uses: “A company wants to turn recordings of customer phone calls into written text. Which AWS service should it use?” The options are Amazon Polly, Amazon Transcribe, Amazon Rekognition and Amazon Personalize.
lab.task: You don't know any of these services yet. Guess anyway. Which word in the question does the work, and which name sounds like it does that job? Commit before you read on.

blocks.text: The AWS Certified AI Practitioner exam, code AIF-C01, is aimed at someone who “uses but does not necessarily build AI/ML solutions on AWS”. The guide lists what's out of scope for you: coding models or algorithms, data engineering, tuning models, and building pipelines or infrastructure. That's the engineers' whole job. What's left is judgement. Given a business problem, pick the approach, the service, the metric or the safety control that fits.

The basics. You get 65 questions in 90 minutes. It costs 100 US dollars, and you sit it at a Pearson VUE test centre or online with a remote proctor watching through your webcam. Only 50 questions count. The other 15 are unscored trial questions, and nothing tells you which ones they are. Scores run from 100 to 1,000, and 700 passes. The scoring is compensatory, so you don't have to pass each topic separately. Unanswered questions are marked wrong, and there is no penalty for guessing. Never leave a blank.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Your video course, recorded in 2024, warns you to expect case study questions: one long scenario followed by several questions about it. What does the current exam guide say?

options.text: Case studies are in. Practise long scenarios.
options.why: This was true on paper once. AWS's 2024 launch blog announced case studies for this exam. The current guide doesn't list them.

options.text: It lists four types: multiple choice, multiple response, ordering and matching. No case study.
options.why: Right. Version 1.1 of the guide names exactly those four. The guide is AWS's official description of the exam, so it wins.

options.text: Only multiple choice. The other formats were dropped.
options.why: Too far the other way. Multiple response, ordering and matching are all still in the guide.

options.text: It doesn't say. You find out on the day.
options.why: The guide spells out each type and how it's scored. You'll see them all in a minute.

verdict.headline: B. Four types, and the guide beats everything else
verdict.body: The guide changed in 2026. Version 1.0 came out on March 26 and version 1.1 on April 30. AWS publishes a guide about a month before the exam changes to match it. So most videos, books and practice sites were written for an older exam. When a source disagrees with the guide, believe the guide. This course is written to version 1.1.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you trusted a source that was right when it was made. That's the exact trap, and now you'll check dates on everything.

blocks.title: The four question types
blocks.intro: Each one is scored all or nothing. There's no partial credit for being nearly right.

steps.d: One correct answer and three wrong ones. The wrong ones are called distractors. They're usually real AWS services doing a different job, chosen because beginners mix them up.
Five or more options, two or more correct. The question says how many, like “(Choose TWO.)”. You must pick every correct one to get the mark. One right and one wrong scores zero.
A list of 3 to 5 responses that complete a task, such as the steps of building a model. You pick the right ones and put them in the right order. One step out of place and the whole question is wrong.
A list of 3 to 7 prompts and a list of responses, such as use cases and services. You match every pair. Get all of them right or get no credit.

steps.t: How this course handles the last two
steps.d: Our practice player shows multiple choice and multiple response. Ordering and matching knowledge gets tested as “Which sequence is correct?” or “Which pairing is correct?” The facts are the same. Only the clicking differs.

blocks.text: The scored questions are split across five domains, and the split is fixed. Fundamentals of AI and ML is 20%. Fundamentals of Generative AI is 24%. Applications of Foundation Models is 28%, the biggest. Guidelines for Responsible AI is 14%, and Security, Compliance and Governance for AI Solutions is 14%. Generative AI and building on it make up over half the exam. This course starts elsewhere, with what a model is, because nothing else makes sense without it.

blocks.title: Whatever older material says about the dropped tools
blocks.text: Version 1.1 removed PartyRock, SageMaker Data Wrangler, SageMaker Feature Store, SageMaker Model Monitor, Bedrock Agents and a metric called AUC from the objectives. If your notes from an older course cover them, don't revise them. They won't be tested. Spend that time on what the guide added instead: agents, a connection standard called MCP, and tools like Kiro and AgentCore, all coming later in this course.

blocks.label: Now the one that costs people marks
blocks.question: An ordering question asks you to put four steps in order. You're sure of three but unsure where the fourth goes. What happens if you get just that one wrong?

options.text: You get three quarters of the mark.
options.why: That's how a lot of school tests work. Not this one. The guide says you must place the responses in the correct order to get credit.

options.text: You get no credit for the question.
options.why: Right. Ordering, matching and multiple response are all or nothing. Close counts for zero.

options.text: You lose points for the wrong step.
options.why: There's no negative marking anywhere on this exam. A wrong answer scores the same as a blank, which is zero.

options.text: It's unscored, so it doesn't matter.
options.why: It might be one of the 15 unscored questions, but you can't tell which ones those are. Treat every question as if it counts.

verdict.headline: B. All or nothing, but never a penalty
verdict.body: Two rules work together here. There's no partial credit, so precision matters on the multi-part types. And there's no penalty for guessing, so you still answer everything. Take your best order and move on. A guess can only help you.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you now know the exam is stricter than it looks. That will make you slow down on exactly the right questions.

blocks.intro: Every question in this course gets read the same way. Find the hint words, cross out the wrong answers with a reason, then pick. Here's a taste of the hint words you'll learn to spot.

rows.tag: “no labelled data”

rows.tag: “company documents, no retraining”

rows.tag: “an exact result is required”

rows.tag: “LEAST operational overhead”
rows.text: Pick the option where AWS does the most of the running for you, usually a managed service.

rows.tag: Trap: a service you learned for Cloud Practitioner
rows.text: Amazon GuardDuty, AWS WAF, AWS Shield and Amazon Route 53 are out of scope for this exam. If one turns up as an option, it's almost certainly a distractor.

rows.tag: Trap: the name from an old course
rows.text: A tool the current guide dropped won't be the right answer. Check what the guide says, not what you remember from a 2024 video.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Find the two words that decide it. Cross out the rest, each with a reason. When a source disagrees with the v1.1 guide, the guide wins.

blocks.question: So if the whole exam is about picking the right kind of AI, what kinds are there?
body: Vendors use “AI”, “machine learning”, “deep learning” and “generative AI” as if they mean the same thing. On the exam they don't, and the questions test exactly where one ends and the next begins.
It turns out to be one picture: four circles, each sitting inside the last. Then there's agents, which don't fit neatly into any of them.

paras: You're an analyst at a regional bank, and a vendor is pitching a tool to sort incoming customer emails. Slide four has one sentence on it.
“Our AI-powered, machine-learning-driven, deep learning platform uses generative AI and agentic AI to route every message.”
Your manager turns to you and asks the fair question. Is that five technologies, or one technology described five times?
You don't know. And the exam will ask you the same thing, one word at a time.
It's 10am in a glass meeting room. You're the analyst the bank's operations team brings along when a vendor pitches, because you're the one who asks awkward questions.
The vendor sells a tool that sorts customer emails into queues. Slide four fills the screen: “AI-powered, machine-learning-driven, deep learning platform using generative AI and agentic AI.”
Your manager leans over and whispers: “Is that five things?”
You open your mouth, then close it. You've heard all five words a hundred times. You couldn't draw the line between any two of them.
The vendor is moving on to pricing. You have about thirty seconds to work out whether the slide is impressive or empty.

panels.line: “AI-powered. Machine-learning-driven. Deep learning.”
panels.sub: “Generative AI. Agentic AI.”

panels.line: “Is that five things?”
You've heard every word. You can't separate any two.
Four of them fit inside each other, like nesting dolls.
panels.sub: The fifth is something else entirely.

lab.setup: Five terms from a vendor slide: AI, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, agentic AI.
lab.task: Before reading on, try to arrange them. Which ones sit inside which? Is there one that doesn't fit the pattern? Sketch it on paper, then check it against the steps below.

blocks.text: Start with three plain words the exam uses constantly. An algorithm is a method for learning. A model is what you get after the algorithm has studied examples. AWS puts it this way: you give a learning algorithm training data, and “the term ML model refers to the model artifact that is created by the training process.” Think of a new hire. The algorithm is how they learn on the job. The pile of past cases they study is the training data. The experienced employee at the end is the model. Training is the studying. Inferencing is the working day: the model gets a case it has never seen and gives an answer.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: A bank's spam filter learned what spam looks like from thousands of emails that people had already marked “spam” or “not spam”. What is it?

options.text: AI, but not machine learning
options.why: It learned from examples instead of following rules someone typed in. Learning from data is exactly what machine learning means.

options.text: Machine learning, but not AI
options.why: This is the tempting one, as if ML were a rival to AI. It's the other way round. ML sits inside AI.

options.text: Both. Machine learning is a kind of AI.
options.why: Right. It learned from data, so it's ML, and every ML system is also AI.

options.text: Generative AI, because it produces a decision
options.why: A label like “spam” isn't new content. Generative AI creates things, such as text, images or audio.

verdict.headline: C. ML is AI, but not all AI is ML
verdict.body: AWS says it directly: “while machine learning is AI, not all AI activities are machine learning.” AI is the broad goal of making machines do tasks that normally need human intelligence. A hand-written rule like “block any email containing ‘lottery’” can count as AI, but it isn't ML because nothing was learned. The moment the system learns the pattern from examples, it's ML.
verdict.aside: If you picked B, you're in good company. The words are usually said side by side, “AI and ML”, as if they were equals. Now you'll hear the nesting every time.

blocks.title: The four circles, from outside in
blocks.intro: Each circle sits inside the one before it. Then one term that isn't a circle at all.

steps.d: The whole field of making machines do things that normally need human intelligence. It's an umbrella term. Rules written by hand can live here.
Systems that learn from data instead of following rules someone typed. The spam filter lives here. So does a model that predicts next month's sales.

ML that uses neural networks with many layers. A neural network is software loosely inspired by the brain: small units called nodes, connected in layers, passing signals along. Deep learning is especially good with messy data like images and text.

Deep learning that creates new content: conversations, stories, images, video, music. A large language model, or LLM, is the best-known kind. It's a very large deep learning model trained on huge amounts of text, and it's what powers a chatbot.

steps.t: Agentic AI: not a circle, a job
steps.d: An agent is a system that acts on its own to reach a goal. It runs a loop: perceive, reason, act, learn. It uses tools, like looking up an order or issuing a refund, and memory. Usually a generative AI model does the reasoning. Chatbots answer. Agents do.

blocks.text: Two more terms cut across the circles instead of sitting in one. Computer vision is the part of AI that lets computers “derive meaningful information from digital images, videos, and other visual inputs”, like spotting a damaged parcel in a photo. Natural language processing, or NLP, lets computers “interpret, manipulate, and comprehend human language”, like reading an email and working out it's a complaint. They're fields, defined by the kind of data they handle. Today most of the strong ones are built with deep learning, because that's what handles images and text well.

blocks.title: How a neural network does its maths
blocks.text: Somewhere you'll find diagrams of weights, layers and activation functions. Skip them. The guide rules mathematical analysis of models out of scope for you. The exam wants one fact about neural networks: layered nodes, loosely brain-inspired, and many layers makes it deep learning. That's the whole answer.

blocks.label: Now the one the exam loves
blocks.question: The spam filter was trained last year. This morning an email it has never seen arrives, and the filter marks it as spam. What is happening this morning?

options.text: Training
options.why: Training happened last year, when it studied the labelled emails. This morning it isn't learning anything new.

options.text: Inferencing
options.why: Right. The trained model is using what it learned to give an answer about new data.

options.text: Labelling
options.why: Labelling is people marking examples with the right answer before training. The filter is producing an answer, not being given one.

options.text: Fine-tuning
options.why: Fine-tuning adjusts an existing model with extra training. That's still training, and it's for a later episode.

verdict.headline: B. Training is school, inferencing is the job
verdict.body: Training happens once, or now and then, and it's the expensive part. Inferencing happens every time the model is used, which might be millions of times a day. When a question mentions a model making predictions on new data, or a chatbot answering a user, that's inferencing.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you've made the classic mix-up. It sticks now: the new hire studies once, then works every day.

blocks.intro: Definition questions give you a description and ask for the term, or ask how two terms relate. The nesting picture answers most of them.

rows.tag: “learns from data without being explicitly programmed”
rows.text: Machine learning.

rows.tag: “neural networks with many layers”, “images and unstructured text”
rows.text: Deep learning.

rows.tag: “creates new content”, “text, images, audio”
rows.text: Generative AI. An LLM is one kind.

rows.tag: “acts autonomously”, “uses tools”, “completes multi-step tasks toward a goal”
rows.text: Agentic AI.

rows.tag: “the model produces predictions on new data”
rows.text: Inferencing. Studying the labelled examples beforehand is training.

rows.tag: Trap: “generative AI is a separate field from machine learning”
rows.text: Wrong. Generative AI sits inside deep learning, which sits inside ML.

rows.tag: Trap: “all AI systems learn from data”
rows.text: Wrong. Rule-based systems can be AI without learning anything. Only ML learns.

rows.tag: Trap: swapping model and algorithm
rows.text: The algorithm is the learning method. The model is the trained result that gets used for predictions.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: AI contains ML contains deep learning contains generative AI. Agents are built on top: they act, not just answer.

cards.back: The algorithm is the learning method. The model is what training produces, and it's what makes predictions.
Training: learning from examples. Inferencing: using the trained model to answer about new data.
Software loosely inspired by the brain: nodes connected in layers. Many layers makes it deep learning.
AI that gets meaning from images, video and other visual inputs.
Natural language processing. AI that interprets and understands human language.
Large language model. A very large deep learning model trained on huge amounts of text. A kind of generative AI.

blocks.question: So the model learns from data. But what if nobody ever marked the right answers?
body: The spam filter had a head start. Thousands of people had already clicked “spam” or “not spam”, so every example came with its answer attached.

Most company data has no answers attached at all. Millions of rows, photos and call recordings, and nobody has tagged a single one. Can a model learn from that? It can, but not the same way, and the kind of data you hold decides which way.

items.q: Put these in order from biggest to smallest: deep learning, AI, generative AI, machine learning.
items.a: AI, then machine learning, then deep learning, then generative AI. Each one sits inside the one before.

items.q: A trained model reads a customer email it has never seen and tags it “complaint”. Training or inferencing?
items.a: Inferencing. Training was the earlier studying of labelled examples. Using the model on new data is inferencing.

paras: You've just joined the claims team at a car insurer as its first data analyst. On day one, your boss hands you two folders and one sentence: “Use AI on these.”
Folder one holds two million past claims in a spreadsheet. Investigators marked 40,000 of them as fraud over the years.
Folder two holds three years of damage photos. Nobody has tagged a single one. Nobody even knows what's in most of them.
Same company, same week, same request. But these two folders can't be handled the same way, and the difference isn't the AI. It's what's already written next to each row.

It's your first Monday as the data analyst at a mid-sized car insurer. Your boss is friendly, busy and slightly vague. “We've got loads of data,” she says. “Use AI on it. Show me something by the end of the month.”

She shares two folders. The first is a spreadsheet of two million past claims going back a decade. There's a column called “outcome”, and 40,000 rows say “fraud”. Investigators filled that in, one case at a time.

The second folder is photos. Three years of dents, scrapes and smashed bumpers, uploaded by customers. Hundreds of thousands of them, and not one has a tag. Nobody knows which are hail damage and which are fender benders.
You sit down with a coffee and realise the two folders ask for different things. One comes with answers. The other comes with nothing but the pictures.
Which one can teach a model to spot fraud? And what could you possibly learn from the other?

lab.setup: Folder one: two million past insurance claims in a spreadsheet, with an “outcome” column where investigators marked 40,000 as fraud. Folder two: hundreds of thousands of customer damage photos, none tagged.
lab.task: For each folder, write one thing a model could learn from it. Then circle the folder where the model can check its own answers against the truth. That circle is the whole episode.

blocks.text: The one question that decides everything: does each example come with the answer written next to it? That answer is called a label. The claims spreadsheet is labelled data, because every row says “fraud” or “not fraud”. The photos are unlabelled data. They're just pictures. Labelling usually means people did the work by hand, like the investigators here, or like you every time you click “this is spam”.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Your boss wants to sort the untagged photos into natural groups so she can see what kinds of damage customers send. Nobody has said what the groups should be. Which kind of learning fits?

options.text: Supervised learning
options.why: Supervised learning needs a label on every example so the model can check itself. These photos have none.

options.text: Unsupervised learning
options.why: Right. It finds hidden patterns in unlabelled data, such as groups of similar-looking photos.

options.text: Reinforcement learning
options.why: Reinforcement learning learns by trial and error from rewards. Nothing here takes actions or earns points.

options.text: No learning is possible without labels
options.why: That's the intuition, and it's wrong. A model can't learn the right answer without labels, but it can still find structure.

verdict.headline: B. No labels means unsupervised
verdict.body: AWS defines it simply: you train the model “to discover hidden patterns in unlabeled data.” The model might find that one group is shattered glass and another is hail dents. It won't know those names. A person looks at each group and decides what it means. The fraud spreadsheet is the opposite case, and that's supervised learning: you train on input data paired with labelled answers.
verdict.aside: If you picked D, you've spotted the real limit. Without labels there's no right answer to learn. What's left is finding groups, and that turns out to be very useful.

blocks.title: Three ways to learn, by what you hold
blocks.intro: Read the data first. The method follows.

steps.t: You hold examples with answers: supervised
steps.d: Every example is paired with its label. The model learns to go from input to answer, then gives answers for new cases. The fraud spreadsheet. Emails marked spam. Past house sales with their prices. Like a student with an answer key.

steps.t: You hold examples, no answers: unsupervised
steps.d: The model finds structure on its own: groups, patterns, oddities. The untagged photos. Customers nobody has sorted into segments. Like tipping a bag of mixed buttons onto a table and sorting them by what looks alike.

steps.t: You hold no examples, just a goal and a score: reinforcement
steps.d: An agent takes actions in an environment and gets rewards or penalties. It learns by trial and error, aiming for the most reward over time. Like training a dog with treats. AWS lists recommendations, cloud cost optimisation and trading as uses.

Semi-supervised learning mixes the first two. It's handy when you have a few labels and lots of unlabelled data. Foundation models are trained in a self-supervised way on huge amounts of data nobody labelled by hand. More on those later.

blocks.text: The exam also names data by its shape. Structured data “fits neatly into data tables”: numbers, short text and dates. That's also called tabular data, meaning rows and columns, like the claims spreadsheet. Unstructured data doesn't fit a table: audio, video, images and long text documents. The photos are unstructured, and so are call recordings and contracts. Time-series data is measurements in time order, like daily claim counts or a sensor reading every minute. Its classic use is predicting what comes next. Semi-structured sits in between, such as videos with a few structured tags attached.

blocks.title: The names of individual algorithms
blocks.text: AWS pages mention algorithms like logistic regression, decision trees and linear regression. Don't memorise them. Choosing and coding algorithms is out of scope for this exam. The questions ask you to name the type of learning from a description of the data. If a scenario says “labelled”, “unlabelled” or “reward”, you already have your answer.

blocks.label: Now a harder one
blocks.question: A warehouse robot learns the fastest route between shelves. It gains points for quick deliveries and loses points for bumping into things. Nobody gives it example routes. Which kind of learning is this?

options.text: Supervised, because the points tell it right from wrong
options.why: Points aren't labels. Supervised learning needs examples paired with the right answer before training starts. The robot has no example routes.

options.text: Unsupervised, because nobody labelled any routes
options.why: True, there are no labels. But unsupervised learning finds groups in existing data. The robot is taking actions and being scored.

options.text: Reinforcement, because it learns from rewards and penalties
options.why: Right. An agent acting in an environment and chasing the most reward over time is reinforcement learning.

options.text: Deep learning, because a robot is involved
options.why: Deep learning is about how a model is built, using layered neural networks. It doesn't describe how the robot gets its feedback.

verdict.headline: C. Rewards mean reinforcement
verdict.body: The hint words are “points”, “reward”, “penalty” and “trial and error”. AWS describes reinforcement learning as a way to train models “to make decisions to achieve the most optimal results.” The parts to recognise are an agent, an environment, actions and a reward. No answer key and no pile of data to sort. Just try, get scored, adjust.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, the points fooled you into thinking they were labels. A label comes with the example. A reward comes after the action. That difference is the whole question.

blocks.intro: These questions describe the data and ask for the learning type, or describe the data and ask for its type. Spot the one word that gives it away.

rows.tag: “labelled”, “historical data with known outcomes”, “tagged examples”
rows.text: Supervised learning.

rows.tag: “no labelled data”, “discover patterns”, “group similar customers”
rows.text: Unsupervised learning.

rows.tag: “reward”, “trial and error”, “agent takes actions in an environment”
rows.text: Reinforcement learning.

rows.tag: “rows and columns”, “spreadsheet”, “database table”
rows.text: Structured, also called tabular, data.

rows.tag: “photos”, “call recordings”, “PDF contracts”, “free-text emails”
rows.text: Unstructured data.

rows.tag: “readings every minute”, “daily sales for three years”
rows.text: Time-series data.

rows.tag: Trap: reinforcement learning for any feedback
rows.text: Wrong if the feedback is a label that came with the data. That's supervised. Reinforcement needs actions and rewards.

rows.tag: Trap: “unsupervised means no humans are involved”
rows.text: Wrong. It means no labels. People still pick the data and decide what the groups mean.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Answers attached: supervised. No answers: unsupervised. Actions and rewards: reinforcement.

blocks.question: You can now match the data to the method. But should you be using machine learning at all?
body: Back at the insurer, the payroll team hears you're “doing AI” and asks for help. They want a model to work out overtime pay.

Overtime pay follows a written rule, and it has to be exactly right every time. A model gives predictions, and predictions are sometimes wrong. So is this a job for ML, or for something much older and much cheaper?

items.q: An online shop wants to split its customers into groups by buying habits. Nobody has labelled any customer. Which kind of learning?
items.a: Unsupervised. No labels means the model finds its own patterns and groups.

items.q: A model learns from ten years of loan applications, each marked “repaid” or “defaulted”. Which kind of learning?
items.a: Supervised. Every example comes with its answer attached.

items.q: What's the difference between an algorithm and a model?
items.a: The algorithm is the learning method. The model is what training produces, and it's the thing that makes predictions.

paras: A vendor quote lands in your inbox at the car insurer. Six weeks of work and a monthly fee to build “an intelligent overtime engine” for payroll.
You open the payroll spreadsheet it would replace. The overtime column is one formula. Hours over 40, times the hourly rate, times 1.5.
The quote is for a model that would learn that rule from past payslips. And then, like every model, it would sometimes guess.
Nobody wants their pay guessed. So why does this quote exist, and how would you spot the next one?
It's Thursday afternoon. Word has spread that you're the analyst “doing AI”, and the payroll lead stops by your desk with a printout.
It's a vendor quote. Six weeks of work plus a monthly fee for “an intelligent overtime engine”. The board wants AI in every department this year, and payroll feels left out.

You ask to see the current process. She opens a spreadsheet and clicks the overtime column. It's one formula. Hours over 40, times the hourly rate, times 1.5. It has been right every week for eleven years.
The proposed model would learn from old payslips and predict each person's overtime. Mostly it would be right. Some weeks, for someone, it wouldn't.
She looks at you. “So do we sign it?”

panels.line: A quote for “an intelligent overtime engine”.
panels.sub: Six weeks of work. A monthly fee.

panels.line: One spreadsheet formula.
panels.sub: Hours over 40 × rate × 1.5. Right every week for eleven years.

panels.line: It predicts. Predictions are sometimes wrong.
“So do we sign it?”

lab.setup: Four requests reach your desk in one week: calculate overtime pay from hours worked, flag suspicious claims, predict next month's claim volume, and suggest add-on products to customers.
lab.task: Mark each one “ML” or “plain rule”. For each, write the one word that decided it. Then find the one where getting it wrong even once is unacceptable.

blocks.text: AWS's own guidance is blunt: “Not every problem requires ML solutions, and sometimes simpler approaches may be more effective and less costly.” A rule is an instruction someone writes down, like “if hours are over 40, pay time and a half”. ML earns its cost when the pattern is too messy or changes too fast to write down. AWS's example: fraud detection “might benefit from ML due to constantly evolving fraudulent behaviors, while simple inventory management might be better served by a rules-based system.” Fraudsters change tactics every month. Overtime law doesn't.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Which of these four tasks is the worst fit for machine learning?

options.text: Flagging insurance claims that look like fraud
options.why: A strong fit. Fraud patterns keep changing, which is exactly when learning from data beats a fixed rule.

options.text: Calculating overtime pay from hours worked
options.why: Right. There's a known rule and the answer must be exact every time. A prediction adds cost and risk and buys nothing.

options.text: Predicting next month's claim volume
options.why: A good fit. Forecasting from past numbers is a classic ML job, and nobody expects a forecast to be exact.

options.text: Recommending add-on products to each customer
options.why: A good fit. Recommendation systems are one of the exam's named ML applications, and a slightly off suggestion does no harm.

verdict.headline: B. When you need a specific outcome, not a prediction
verdict.body: The exam guide names two reasons ML is not appropriate. One is when “a specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction”. The other is a cost-benefit analysis that doesn't add up. ML needs data preparation, computing power and ongoing maintenance, and AWS says that cost “must be justified by the business value it delivers.” Overtime fails both tests: it needs an exact answer, and a free formula already gives it.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you may have thought fraud was too serious to leave to a model. Seriousness isn't the test. Whether you can write the rule down is.

blocks.title: Three jobs a model can do
blocks.intro: Once ML fits, the exam asks which technique. Look at what the answer looks like.

steps.t: The answer is a number: regression
steps.d: Predicts a value on a scale. Next month's claim volume. The repair cost of a claim in dollars. A house's sale price. It's supervised, so it learns from past examples with known numbers.

steps.t: The answer is a category: classification
steps.d: Predicts which bucket something belongs in. Fraud or not fraud. Spam or not spam. Which of five complaint types an email is. Also supervised. Think of a mail room sorting letters into labelled trays.

steps.t: There's no answer yet, just groups: clustering
steps.d: Groups similar items together without being told the groups. Customers with similar habits. Photos that look alike. It's unsupervised, the method from last episode, and a person names the groups afterwards.
“Will this customer cancel?” sounds like a prediction about the future, so people reach for regression. But the answer is yes or no. Two categories means classification.

blocks.text: Where does AI add value? The guide names three kinds. It assists human decisions, like flagging risky claims for an investigator to review rather than rejecting them automatically. It scales, handling a million emails as easily as a hundred. And it automates repetitive work. The guide's list of real-world uses is worth knowing by sight: computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, recommendation systems, fraud detection, forecasting, knowledge bases and agentic AI. Knowledge bases are collections of documents a system can search to answer questions. Every one of these is a job where the pattern is too messy for a rule.

blocks.title: Every other technique name you'll find
blocks.text: AWS pages also describe association rules, which find links like “people who buy X often buy Y”. Interesting, but the guide only asks you to pick between regression, classification and clustering. Learn those three cold and don't collect more. On this exam, a wider vocabulary just gives you more wrong answers to choose from.

blocks.label: Now the one the exam loves
blocks.question: The insurer wants to predict how much each new car claim will cost to settle, in dollars, using thousands of past claims with their final costs. Which technique fits?

options.text: Classification
options.why: Classification picks a category. A dollar amount isn't a category, it's a number on a scale.

options.text: Regression
options.why: Right. The answer is a number, and the past claims come with known costs. Supervised, predicting a value.

options.text: Clustering
options.why: Clustering groups similar claims but never predicts a cost. It also ignores the known costs, which are the most useful part of this data.

options.text: A rules-based system
options.why: Settlement cost depends on too many shifting factors to write as one formula. There's no exact rule to follow, so a prediction is what's needed.

verdict.headline: B. A number means regression
verdict.body: Ask one question: what shape is the answer? A number on a scale is regression. A label from a fixed list is classification. Groups nobody named yet is clustering. If the question hands you past examples with known dollar amounts, it's regression every time.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you may have pictured sorting claims into “cheap” and “expensive”. That would be classification. The question asked for the dollar figure, which makes it regression.

blocks.intro: These questions describe a business need and ask which technique fits, or whether ML fits at all. The shape of the answer gives it away.

rows.tag: “predict a price”, “how many”, “how much”, “forecast sales”
rows.text: Regression. The answer is a number.

rows.tag: “fraud or not”, “which category”, “spam”, “will the customer churn”
rows.text: Classification. The answer is a label, even when it's yes or no.

rows.tag: “group similar customers”, “segment”, “no labels”
rows.text: Clustering.

rows.tag: “exact result required”, “fixed business rule”, “must be the same every time”
rows.text: Not ML. A rules-based approach is cheaper and always right.

rows.tag: “patterns change constantly”, “too many factors to write rules for”
rows.text: ML adds value here.

rows.tag: Trap: ML as the answer to every scenario
rows.text: On an AI exam it feels like the answer must be AI. When the need is an exact, known outcome, the right answer is the simple rule.

rows.tag: Trap: regression for yes-or-no predictions
rows.text: “Will they cancel?” is about the future, but the answer is a category. That's classification.

rows.tag: Trap: clustering when labels exist
rows.text: If the data already has the answers, use them. Clustering throws them away.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Exact answer needed: a rule. A number: regression. A category: classification. Groups with no labels: clustering.

blocks.question: So ML fits your problem. Do you have to build the model yourself?
body: Everything so far assumed someone gathers data, picks a technique and trains a model. That's months of work and a team you probably don't have.

For some of the most common jobs, AWS has already done it. There are ready-made services that hear, speak, read and see, and you just send them your data. The trick is telling them apart, because their names don't always say what they do.

episodes.title: Transcribe hears, Polly speaks, Rekognition sees
episodes.deck: The pre-trained AI services. Learn the verb, not the name.

items.q: A chatbot is answering a customer's question right now. Is the model training or inferencing?
items.a: Inferencing. Training is when a model learns from data. Inferencing is when the finished model gets new input and gives an answer.

items.q: A shop wants to split its customers into groups, but nobody has ever labelled which group anyone belongs to. Which kind of learning fits?
items.a: Unsupervised learning. With no labels, the model finds the hidden patterns itself. Grouping like this is called clustering.

items.q: A tax rule must give exactly the same answer for the same input, every time. ML or a plain rule?
items.a: A plain rule. ML makes predictions. When a specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction, ML is the wrong tool.

paras: A car insurer's call centre records 10,000 calls a week. Somewhere in them are the customers about to leave, the claims going wrong, and the agent who keeps promising things the policy doesn't cover. Nobody has time to listen to any of it.
The calls aren't the only pile. Claims also arrive as photos of dented bumpers, scanned forms with handwriting in the boxes, and emails in Spanish.

Your boss wants the angry callers found by Friday. You don't have a data scientist, and you don't have a year. You don't need either. AWS has already trained a model for each of those jobs. The hard part is knowing which one does which.
There are eight names to learn, and most sound nothing like what they do. So don't learn names. Learn verbs.

You started in claims operations at a car insurer three weeks ago. This morning your manager forwards you one number with one line underneath: "10,000 recorded calls last week. Which ones were angry? Can AI do this?"

You open a few recordings. A man who is very upset about his tow truck. A woman who has phoned three times about the same claim. Then you look at the rest of the claims inbox: a photo of a crumpled wing mirror, a scanned form filled in by hand with a table of repair costs, an email that starts "Buenos días".

Your first thought is that this needs a team of engineers and a year. Your second thought, after lunch with someone from IT, is that it doesn't. AWS sells models that are already trained for each of these jobs. You just send them the file.

The catch is the names. Transcribe, Comprehend, Textract, Rekognition. You need to know which one listens to the calls and which one reads the form. You write four verbs on a sticky note: hear, understand, read, see.

lab.setup: A car insurer records 10,000 calls a week. Its claims inbox also holds photos of damaged cars, handwritten scanned forms with tables, and emails in Spanish.
lab.task: For each of the four inputs, write the one verb the AI has to do: hear, see, read a form, or translate. Then guess which AWS service name matches each verb. Check your guesses against the list below.

blocks.text: Every service in this episode is a pre-trained AI service. AWS built and trained the model. You send it data through an API (a doorway one program uses to ask another program for something) and get an answer back. No training, and no servers to run. Think of a specialist contractor instead of a new hire. The contractor turns up already knowing the job, and only does that one job. So nearly every exam question here is really asking one thing: what verb does the scenario need?

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The insurer wants to find which of last week's recorded phone calls came from angry customers. Which approach fits?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend on the recordings
options.why: Close. Comprehend reads the mood of text, but a recording is audio. Something has to turn the speech into words first.

options.text: Amazon Transcribe to turn the calls into text, then Amazon Comprehend to read the sentiment
options.why: Right. Transcribe hears, Comprehend understands. Two verbs, so two services.

options.text: Amazon Polly
options.why: Polly goes the other way. It turns text into speech, so it would read the complaints out loud, not analyse them.

options.text: Amazon Lex
options.why: Lex builds chatbots that hold a conversation. There's no conversation here, just old recordings to analyse.

verdict.headline: B. Audio needs hearing before it needs understanding
verdict.body: Comprehend works on text. Transcribe converts audio to text. When a scenario starts with audio and ends with meaning, you need both, in that order. The exam likes this chain because each half on its own looks almost right.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you've found the most common mix-up in this whole topic. You won't make it on exam day.

blocks.title: Eight services, eight verbs
blocks.intro: One line each. The verb is what you memorise.

steps.d: Speech to text. It uses automatic speech recognition to turn audio into a transcript, either live (streaming) or in a batch of recordings. Call centre recordings are the classic case.
Text to lifelike speech. Reading articles aloud, talking menus, accessibility. It's the mirror image of Transcribe.
Text in one language, text out in another. Multilingual chat, websites, support emails.

Natural language processing (NLP, software that works with human language) on text you already have. It finds sentiment, key phrases, names of people and places, personal data such as phone numbers, and the language a text is written in.
Builds chatbots and phone bots that talk with people by voice or text. It works out what the person wants and asks follow-up questions.
Image and video analysis. It spots objects and scenes, flags unsafe content, compares faces, and can find text in a photo, like a street sign.
Pulls typed and handwritten text out of scanned documents, and keeps the structure: form fields, tables, invoices, ID documents.
"Customers who viewed this also viewed." It generates item recommendations for each user, learned from your own data about who clicked or bought what.

blocks.text: Real scenarios chain these together. Picture a claims phone line. Lex runs the conversation: it hears the caller, works out that they want to report a claim, and asks for the policy number. If the caller speaks Spanish, Translate sits in the middle. Polly gives Lex's replies a voice. Personalize is the odd one out in the list. Instead of arriving fully trained, it learns from your own customers' behaviour. It's still fully managed, so you don't build the model yourself.

blocks.title: The services AWS has closed, and the feature menus
blocks.text: Older study guides also teach Amazon Kendra, Forecast, Fraud Detector and the Lookout family; Kendra, Forecast and Fraud Detector are now closed to new customers, the Lookout services are retired or retiring, and none of them is on the v1.1 in-scope list. Skip each service's full feature list too. Comprehend alone has a long list of features. The exam asks for the verb, not the menu.

blocks.label: Now the pair the exam loves
blocks.question: The insurer receives scanned claim forms. Customers fill in the boxes by hand, and each form has a table of repair costs. The insurer wants the fields and the table as data it can store. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon Rekognition
options.why: Tempting, because Rekognition can find text in an image. But it spots words in a picture. It doesn't understand that a box is a form field or that rows belong to a table.

options.text: Amazon Textract
options.why: Right. Textract extracts typed and handwritten text from documents and keeps the forms and tables intact.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
options.why: Comprehend analyses text you already have. A scanned form is still just a picture until something extracts the text from it.

options.text: Amazon Transcribe
options.why: Transcribe handles audio. Nothing in this scenario makes a sound.

verdict.headline: B. Documents mean Textract
verdict.body: Rekognition sees what's in a photo. Textract reads documents. The hint words are "form", "table", "invoice", "scanned" and "handwritten". If the picture is a document, pick Textract. If it's a scene, a face or a product, pick Rekognition.
verdict.aside: If you picked Rekognition, you spotted something true: it can read text. That's exactly why the exam uses it as a distractor.

blocks.intro: These questions describe the input and the output, then ask for the service. Find the verb and the answer follows.

rows.tag: "call recordings", "audio to text", "subtitles", "speech recognition"
rows.text: Amazon Transcribe.

rows.tag: "read aloud", "lifelike voice", "text to speech"
rows.text: Amazon Polly.

rows.tag: "sentiment", "key phrases", "entities", "detect PII in text"
rows.text: Amazon Comprehend.

rows.tag: "chatbot", "conversational interface", "voice bot for the call centre"
rows.text: Amazon Lex.

rows.tag: "scanned forms", "tables", "invoices", "handwriting"
rows.text: Amazon Textract.

rows.tag: "faces", "objects in images", "unsafe content in video"
rows.text: Amazon Rekognition.

rows.tag: Trap: Comprehend for audio sentiment
rows.text: Wrong on its own. Comprehend reads text, so audio goes through Transcribe first.

rows.tag: Trap: Polly to build a chatbot
rows.text: Wrong. Polly only speaks. Lex holds the conversation, and it can hand its replies to Polly.

rows.tag: Trap: Comprehend to translate a review
rows.text: Wrong. Comprehend can tell you which language a text is in. Translate converts it.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Name the verb in the scenario: hear, speak, translate, understand, converse, see, read a document, recommend. Each verb has exactly one service.

cards.back: Hears. Speech to text, live or in batches.
Speaks. Text to lifelike speech.
Translates text from one language to another.
Understands text: sentiment, key phrases, entities, PII, language.
Converses. Builds voice and text chatbots.
Sees. Objects, faces and unsafe content in images and video.
Reads documents. Text, forms and tables from scans, including handwriting.
Recommends items to each user, learned from your own data.

blocks.question: These models arrived trained. What happens when you have to train your own?
body: Pre-trained services cover the common jobs. But no AWS service knows which of your customers are about to cancel. For that you build a model from your own data.
And a model you build has a problem the contractors don't. It's right on the day you ship it. Six months later, with nobody touching it, it can be quietly wrong.

episodes.title: From raw data to a model that's still right next month
episodes.deck: The pipeline, MLOps, and the four ways to ask a model a question.

items.q: Which AWS service turns text into speech, and which one does the reverse?
items.a: Amazon Polly speaks: text in, voice out. Amazon Transcribe hears: audio in, text out.

items.q: You have 50,000 support tickets with no tags, and you want to find natural groups in them. Supervised or unsupervised learning?
items.a: Unsupervised. There are no labels to learn from, so the model finds the groups itself. That's clustering.

items.q: Deep learning sits inside which circle, and what sits inside deep learning?
items.a: Deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI. Generative AI sits inside deep learning.

paras: In January, the data team at a meal-kit company shipped a model that predicts which subscribers will cancel. It was right about 8 times in 10. The retention team sent discount codes to everyone it flagged, and cancellations dropped.
By June, the model is barely better than a coin flip. The discounts are going to loyal customers who were never leaving. The ones actually leaving get nothing.
Nobody changed a line of code. The model is exactly the model it was in January.
That's the problem. In March the company doubled its menu and raised prices. Its customers started behaving differently, and the model is still predicting January's customers.
You're the analyst who looks after the retention dashboard at a meal-kit company. It's June, and the head of retention has booked 30 minutes with you. The calendar invite just says "the model??"

You remember January well. The data team shipped a model that scored every subscriber on how likely they were to cancel. It was right about 8 times in 10. Discount codes went to the risky ones, and the cancellation line on your dashboard bent downwards.
Now the line is going back up. You pull a sample of flagged customers. Half of them have ordered every week for two years. Meanwhile, three people who cancelled yesterday were scored as safe.
You ask the data team what changed. "Nothing," they say. "Same model, same code."
Then you remember March. The company doubled its menu and raised prices. Your customers changed. The model didn't.

panels.line: A model predicts who will cancel.
panels.sub: Right about 8 times in 10.

panels.line: Menu doubles. Prices go up.
The model is a coin flip.
panels.sub: Discounts go to loyal customers. The leavers get nothing.

panels.line: "We haven't changed anything."
panels.sub: That's exactly what went wrong.

lab.setup: A model that predicts subscriber cancellations was right 8 times in 10 in January. In March the company changed its menu and prices. By June the model is barely better than guessing. Its code has not changed.
lab.task: Write down what you think broke, and what the team should have had in place to notice it in April instead of June. Then read on.

blocks.text: A model is a snapshot. Training freezes whatever patterns were in the data at the time, like a map drawn in January. When the roads change, the map doesn't redraw itself. That's why AWS treats a model as a loop, not a project with an end date. Its machine learning guidance says the stages "are not necessarily sequential in nature and can have feedback loops".

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Why did the meal-kit model go from 8 in 10 to a coin flip?

options.text: The live data drifted away from the data it was trained on
options.why: Right. Customers changed after March, and the model still reflects January. Monitoring compares live data with training data to catch exactly this.

options.text: The model slowly forgot what it learned
options.why: A trained model doesn't change on its own. Nothing faded. The model stayed the same while the world moved.

options.text: The servers got slower
options.why: Slow servers make answers late, not wrong. This model answers quickly. It just answers for a world that's gone.

options.text: It was trained with too little data
options.why: Then it would have been bad in January too. It was good at launch and got worse later, which points at a change in the data.

verdict.headline: A. The world moved, the model didn't
verdict.body: This is called drift. The live data no longer looks like the training data, so the predictions quietly get worse. The fix isn't to repair the model. It's to watch it (monitoring) and to retrain it on fresh data when it slips.
verdict.aside: If you picked B, it's a very human guess. People forget. Models don't, and that's the problem.

blocks.title: The pipeline, one stage at a time
blocks.intro: These stages come from AWS's Well-Architected guidance for machine learning. The last arrow points back to the start.

steps.d: What decision should this help with, and how will you know it worked? "Cut cancellations by a tenth" is a goal. "Use AI" isn't.
Turn the goal into a prediction. "Will this subscriber cancel in the next 30 days, yes or no?" is a classification problem.
Collect it, clean it, and do feature engineering: create and pick the columns that help the model, like "days since last order".
Train it on past data, tune it, then evaluate it on data it hasn't seen yet. Episode 7 covers the scores.
Put the model where apps can send it new data and get predictions back. This is inference.
Check that it's still performing. Compare live data with training data, and compare predictions with what actually happened. When it slips, go back to step 3 and retrain.

blocks.text: Step 5 has a choice hidden in it. With a managed API service, a provider runs the model, and you send requests and get answers. Amazon Bedrock works like this for foundation models. With a self-hosted API, the model is deployed and managed by the organisation using it, for example on endpoints you set up in Amazon SageMaker AI. Managed means less work. Self-hosted means more control and more to look after.

Doing that loop by hand once is a science project. Doing it every month without mistakes is MLOps: "a set of practices that automate and simplify machine learning workflows and deployments." It's the kitchen routine that lets a restaurant cook the same dish on a busy Saturday. The exam's list: experimentation (try ideas and record what you tried), repeatable processes (version the data and code so a training run can be reproduced and audited), scalable systems, managing technical debt (the shortcuts, like one person's manual script, that cost you later), production readiness, model monitoring, and model retraining. The meal-kit team was missing the last two.

blocks.title: Four ways to ask a model a question
blocks.intro: Once a model is deployed, the scenario tells you how it gets asked. Match the timing words.

steps.d: One request, answer in a moment, someone waiting. For interactive, low-latency work, like checking a card payment while the customer stands at the till.
Also on demand, but you manage no infrastructure. Fits traffic that comes in spurts with idle periods between, as long as an occasional slow first answer (a cold start) is acceptable.
Requests go into a queue and get processed in turn. For large inputs and long processing times when "soon" is good enough.
A whole dataset at once, with nothing left running afterwards. Scoring every subscriber overnight is batch. Amazon Bedrock also offers batch inference for large sets of prompts.

blocks.title: A tool name for every pipeline stage
blocks.text: Older study guides pin a named SageMaker tool to each stage of the pipeline. The v1.1 guide dropped that list. For this objective it now names four services only: Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Quick, Kiro and Amazon SageMaker AI, and episode 8 covers them. Learn what each stage is for, not a product per stage.

blocks.label: Now the one the exam loves
blocks.question: A hospital uploads large medical scans one at a time throughout the day for a model to analyse. Each scan takes several minutes to process. Staff are happy to get results a little later, but not the next day. Which type of inference fits?

options.text: Real-time inference
options.why: Real-time is for quick, interactive answers. Minutes of processing per large file is not what it's built for.

options.text: Asynchronous inference
options.why: Right. Large inputs, long processing, and "a little later" is fine. The requests queue up and get answered in turn.

options.text: Batch inference
options.why: Batch is for scoring a big dataset in one go. Scans arrive one at a time through the day and staff want each result the same day.

options.text: Serverless inference
options.why: Serverless is about spiky traffic and no infrastructure to manage. It doesn't address large files with long processing times.

verdict.headline: B. Big and slow, but still today: asynchronous
verdict.body: Read the timing words. "Immediately" or "low latency" means real-time. "Idle periods" or "intermittent traffic" means serverless. "Large payload" or "long processing" with "near real-time" means asynchronous. "Overnight", "entire dataset" or "no persistent endpoint" means batch.
verdict.aside: If you picked batch, you were half right. Both handle big work. The difference is one request at a time through the day versus a whole pile at once.

blocks.intro: These questions describe a symptom or a timing need and ask for the stage, the practice or the inference type.

rows.tag: "accuracy dropped after launch", "customer behaviour changed"
rows.text: Drift. Monitor the model and retrain it on fresh data.

rows.tag: "reproducible", "auditable", "repeatable", "automate the workflow"
rows.text: MLOps: version the data and code, and automate the steps.

rows.tag: "no infrastructure to manage", "intermittent traffic", "tolerate cold starts"
rows.text: Serverless inference.

rows.tag: "score millions of records overnight"
rows.text: Batch inference.

rows.tag: Trap: "retrain once at launch and you're done"
rows.text: Wrong. The lifecycle loops. Monitoring and retraining are standing jobs.

rows.tag: Trap: real-time inference for a nightly job
rows.text: Wrong. Nobody is waiting on each answer, so a persistent low-latency endpoint wastes money. Use batch.

rows.tag: Trap: "self-hosted means less to manage"
rows.text: Wrong. Self-hosted means your organisation deploys and runs the model. A managed API is the low-effort option.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: A model is a snapshot of the past. Monitor it, retrain it, and pick the inference type from the timing words in the question.

blocks.question: The meal-kit model was "right 8 times in 10". Right about what?
body: Suppose only 1 subscriber in 100 ever cancels. A model that says "nobody will cancel" is right 99 times in 100. It's also useless.
So the headline score on a model can look brilliant and mean nothing. Next time: the numbers that tell you whether a model actually works.

episodes.title: Ninety-nine per cent accurate and completely useless
episodes.deck: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 — and the business metrics that decide if it was worth it.

items.q: A retailer scores every customer overnight and needs the results by morning. Nobody is waiting on any single answer. Which type of inference fits?
items.a: Batch inference. It handles a whole dataset at once and leaves nothing running afterwards.

items.q: A model was right at launch and is wrong six months later. Nobody changed the code. What happened, and what's the fix?
items.a: Drift. The live data stopped looking like the training data. The fix is monitoring, then retraining on fresh data.

items.q: Fraud detection or simple inventory reordering: which one is the better fit for ML?
items.a: Fraud detection, because fraudsters keep changing their behaviour. AWS's own example says simple inventory management may be better served by rules.

paras: You're two months into an analyst job at a card-payments startup. A vendor is pitching a fraud model, and the slide on the screen says one thing, in very large type: 99% accurate.
Your head of risk looks impressed. You do some arithmetic on a napkin.
About 1 transaction in 100 at your company is fraud. So a "model" that stamps every single transaction "fine" would be right 99 times in 100. It would also be 99% accurate.
It would never catch a single fraud. You raise your hand and ask the vendor one question: of the frauds, how many did it catch?
It's a Thursday afternoon at a card-payments startup, and you're in the back row of a vendor pitch. You're the newest analyst. You were invited to take notes.
The vendor gets to the slide everyone came for. A single number, 99%, and the word "accurate" underneath. The head of risk leans forward.

You look at last month's figures on your laptop. 10,000 transactions. 100 of them were fraud. You try something. If you wrote a program that said "not fraud" to every transaction, how often would it be right? 9,900 times out of 10,000. That's 99%.
Your program would be exactly as accurate as their model. It would also let all 100 frauds through.
You put your hand up. "Of the 100 frauds, how many did your model catch?" The vendor clicks to a slide that isn't in the deck.

panels.line: "Our fraud model is 99% accurate."
10,000 transactions. 100 are fraud.
panels.sub: So a model that says "fine" to everything is right 9,900 times.

panels.line: 99% accurate.
Zero.
panels.sub: So what does 99% actually tell you?

lab.setup: Out of 10,000 card transactions, 100 are fraud. Model X labels every transaction "not fraud". Model Y flags 150 transactions, and 90 of those are really fraud.
lab.task: Work out how many transactions each model gets right out of 10,000. Then decide which model you'd buy, and write down why the accuracy numbers alone don't tell you.

blocks.text: Every prediction a fraud model makes lands in one of four boxes. Think of a smoke alarm. It goes off and there's a fire: a true positive. It goes off because you burned toast: a false positive, a false alarm. It stays silent while the kitchen burns: a false negative, a miss. It stays silent and nothing's wrong: a true negative. Lay those four counts out in a grid and you have a confusion matrix. Every metric in this episode is just a different way of reading that grid.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Model X says "not fraud" to all 10,000 transactions and scores 99% accuracy. Which number exposes it?

options.text: Recall: of the 100 real frauds, how many it caught
options.why: Right. Model X caught 0 of 100. Its recall is 0%, and no amount of accuracy hides that.

options.text: Accuracy on a bigger test set
options.why: More data gives the same answer. If 1% is fraud, the do-nothing model stays about 99% accurate however many transactions you test.

options.text: The number of transactions it processes per second
options.why: That measures speed, not whether it's right. Model X is very fast. It never has to think.

options.text: Precision: of the transactions it flagged, how many were really fraud
options.why: Close, but Model X flagged nothing, so there's nothing to check. Precision tells you about false alarms, and Model X never raises one.

verdict.headline: A. Recall asks about the ones that got away
verdict.body: Accuracy counts every correct answer, and when 99% of cases are "fine", saying "fine" is easy. This is called an imbalanced dataset, and it's where accuracy lies. Recall only looks at the real frauds and asks how many the model found. It's the metric AWS uses for cancer testing, where the goal is "to find all of the true positives".
verdict.aside: If you picked D, you were one box away. Precision and recall are the pair everyone swaps, which is why the next section pulls them apart.

blocks.title: Model Y, read four ways
blocks.intro: 10,000 transactions, 100 of them fraud. Model Y flags 150. Of those 150, 90 are really fraud and 60 are false alarms. It misses 10 frauds.

steps.d: It gets 9,930 of 10,000 right: the 90 frauds it caught, plus 9,840 legitimate transactions it left alone. Barely higher than Model X's 99%, even though Model Y is far more useful.
Of the 150 it flagged, 90 were really fraud. Precision asks: when the alarm goes off, how often is there a fire? It matters most when a false alarm is expensive.
Of the 100 real frauds, it caught 90. Recall asks: of all the fires, how many did the alarm catch? It matters most when a miss is expensive.

One score that combines precision and recall. It stays low unless both are high, so a model can't game it by flagging everything or nothing. Use it when you need one number and both kinds of mistake hurt.

blocks.text: There's a trap underneath all four numbers. Where did you measure them? A model can score brilliantly on the data it trained on and badly on anything new. That's overfitting: it memorised the practice questions instead of learning the subject. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to find the pattern at all, so it does badly everywhere. You'll meet both properly in episode 23. For now, one habit: trust scores measured on data the model has never seen.

blocks.title: AUC and the formulas
blocks.text: Older study guides teach AUC, a score drawn from a curve of true alarms against false alarms. The v1.1 guide removed it and added precision and recall instead, so leave it alone. Skip the formulas too. The exam won't ask you to calculate F1. It asks which metric fits a scenario, and for that you need the smoke alarm, not the algebra.

blocks.label: Now flip the cost
blocks.question: A law firm builds a spam filter. The worst outcome is a real client's email landing in the spam folder and going unread. Which metric should the firm care about most?

options.text: Recall
options.why: Recall is about catching every piece of spam. That matters less here. A bit of spam in the inbox is annoying, not a disaster.

options.text: Accuracy
options.why: Accuracy lumps both mistakes together. The firm cares about one specific mistake, so it needs the metric that isolates it.

options.text: Precision
options.why: Right. A client email in spam is a false positive, a false alarm. Precision asks: of the emails marked spam, how many really were? High precision means few real emails get binned.

options.text: Processing speed
options.why: A fast filter that bins client emails is just a fast way to lose clients. Speed doesn't measure which mistakes it makes.

verdict.headline: C. When false alarms hurt, precision
verdict.body: Ask which mistake is the expensive one. False alarms expensive, like a real email binned or an innocent customer's card blocked: precision. Misses expensive, like fraud getting through or a sick patient sent home: recall. Both expensive and you want one number: F1. AWS's own wording is that precision matters "when the cost of a false positive is high".
verdict.aside: If you picked recall, flip the question around: what does the filter do wrong that the firm can't live with? That one question settles every precision-or-recall item.

blocks.text: Model Y is better. Is it worth buying? That's a different question, and model metrics can't answer it. The exam names four business metrics for it. Development costs: what it took to build. Cost per user: what it costs to run for each customer. Customer feedback: whether 60 false alarms a month means 60 angry customers with blocked cards. Return on investment (ROI): what you gain, like the frauds stopped, compared with what you spent. A model with a 90% recall that costs more than the fraud it stops is a bad buy.

blocks.intro: These questions describe which mistake hurts and ask for the metric, or describe a business question and ask for the business metric.

rows.tag: "false positives are costly", "don't block legitimate customers"
rows.text: Precision.

rows.tag: "must not miss", "find all the cases", "false negatives are costly"
rows.text: Recall.

rows.tag: "balance precision and recall", "a single score"
rows.text: F1 score.

rows.tag: "was it worth the investment", "cost per user", "customer feedback"
rows.text: Business metrics such as ROI, not model metrics.

rows.tag: "great on training data, poor on new data"
rows.text: Overfitting.

rows.tag: Trap: accuracy for rare events like fraud or disease
rows.text: Wrong. When one outcome is rare, a model that always predicts the common one looks accurate and catches nothing.

rows.tag: Trap: recall when false alarms are the problem
rows.text: Wrong way round. Recall is about misses. False alarms are precision's job.

rows.tag: Trap: AUC as the answer
rows.text: Dropped from the v1.1 guide. If it appears as an option, it's almost certainly a distractor.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Name the expensive mistake. False alarms: precision. Misses: recall. Both: F1. Worth the money: ROI.

blocks.question: You can grade a model now. But should your company build one at all?
body: Model Y came from a vendor who trained it for months. You could build your own. Or you could skip training altogether and rent a foundation model that already knows a lot about everything.
Each choice has a different price. And sometimes the choice isn't yours at all, because a regulator wants you to explain every decision the model makes.

episodes.title: Build it, borrow it, or rent it
episodes.deck: SageMaker AI for your own models, foundation models for everything else — and when a regulator decides for you.

items.q: A fraud model flagged 150 transactions, and 90 of them were really fraud. Which metric is that, and what's the score?
items.a: Precision, at 60%. It asks how often the alarm was right when it went off. Recall asks how many of all the real frauds it caught.

items.q: A company wants to use a model without deploying or running it, just by sending requests to a provider. Managed API service or self-hosted API?
items.a: Managed API service. Self-hosted means your own organisation deploys and manages the model.

items.q: Which service pulls the fields and tables out of a scanned, handwritten form?
items.a: Amazon Textract. Rekognition can spot text in a photo, but only Textract keeps the form and table structure.

paras: You run the tiny technology team at a credit union, and on Monday four people ask you for AI.

The lending manager wants a model to approve or decline small loans. Marketing wants first drafts of product descriptions. The two developers want help writing the new mobile app. The finance director wants to ask questions of her spreadsheets in plain English.
You have one budget and no data scientists. It would be lovely to buy one AI and point it at all four.
Then compliance forwards a note. The regulator expects you to explain every loan you decline, applicant by applicant. One of the four requests just stopped being your choice.
It's Monday at a credit union with 90 staff, and you are the technology team. You and one contractor.

By ten o'clock, four people have stopped by your desk. Priya from lending wants small loans approved or declined automatically. Tom from marketing wants first drafts of product descriptions, because he writes forty a month. The two developers building the new app want an assistant that writes code. And the finance director wants to ask "why did deposits drop in March?" and get an answer, not a pivot table.
You start sketching one big AI that does all four. It's tidy. It's one contract.
At three o'clock, compliance forwards you an email. The regulator expects the credit union to explain every declined loan, applicant by applicant, with reasons.
You look at your sketch again. Three of these jobs can share a tool. One of them can't.

panels.line: Four teams. Four requests for AI.
panels.sub: Loans. Marketing copy. App code. Finance questions.

panels.line: Buy one AI. Point it at everything.
"We must explain every declined loan."
Three jobs can share a tool.

lab.setup: A credit union gets four requests: automatic loan decisions that must be explained to a regulator, marketing copy drafts, help writing app code, and plain-English questions about finance data.
lab.task: Sort the four into two piles: jobs where a general-purpose generative AI is fine, and jobs where it isn't. Write one reason for anything in the second pile.

blocks.text: There are three ways to get a model, and they work like dinner. Build it: train a custom model on your own data, like cooking from scratch. You control every ingredient, and you do all the work. Borrow it: start from an open-source pre-trained model someone else published, then tune it to your needs, like a meal kit. Rent it: call a foundation model (a huge model trained on a massive range of data, ready for many tasks) through a managed API, like ordering takeaway. Fastest to eat, least control over the recipe.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The credit union must explain every declined loan to its regulator. Which approach fits the loan decisions best?

options.text: A traditional ML model trained on the credit union's past loan data, built in Amazon SageMaker AI
options.why: Right. A model trained for one narrow job on your own records is easier to explain and document, which is what regulated decisions need.

options.text: A foundation model in Amazon Bedrock, prompted to decide and to write out its reasons
options.why: Tempting, because it can write reasons in fluent English. But foundation models are often considered black boxes. Fluent reasons it writes aren't proof of how it actually decided.

options.text: An Amazon Quick dashboard of past loan decisions
options.why: A dashboard shows what happened. It doesn't make a decision about a new applicant.

options.text: Kiro
options.why: Kiro helps developers write code. It could help build the loan app, but it isn't the model that decides the loans.

verdict.headline: A. When a regulator asks why, go traditional
verdict.body: The exam gives three reasons to pick traditional ML over a foundation model: regulatory concerns, explainability requirements and operational constraints. Loans hit the first two at once. AWS puts it plainly: "Regulated domains may need reliable explanations for how ML models make predictions." A foundation model is a brilliant generalist, but a generalist is hard to audit.
verdict.aside: If you picked Bedrock, you reached for the most powerful tool in the room. Keep it for the other three requests, where it fits.

blocks.title: Four services, four kinds of user
blocks.intro: The v1.1 guide names four AWS services for this part of the lifecycle. The fastest way to tell them apart is to ask who sits in front of each one.

steps.t: Amazon SageMaker AI: people building their own models
steps.d: A fully managed service to build, train and deploy ML models. It includes Studio (a workspace for ML development), Canvas (build models in a visual interface, no code), JumpStart (a hub of pre-trained, open-source models you can tune before deploying) and Model Registry (keeps track of model versions and approvals). Build and borrow both happen here.

steps.t: Amazon Bedrock: people building apps on foundation models
steps.d: Rent. A fully managed service that gives access to foundation models from many AI companies through one API. Episode 12 covers it properly.
An agentic coding service. It turns prompts into detailed specs, then into working code, docs and tests. It runs on Amazon Bedrock.

An AI-powered service for analysing data, automating tasks, building simple web apps and doing research. It includes Quick Sight for dashboards. Amazon Quick evolved from Amazon QuickSight, so older material uses that name.

blocks.text: One naming change you'll see in the console: on 3 December 2024, Amazon SageMaker was renamed Amazon SageMaker AI. Plain "SageMaker" now means a wider data and analytics platform. The exam says SageMaker AI. The third reason to prefer traditional ML is operations. Larger foundation models are expensive to run, need more computing power, and their complex design can slow down each answer. If a job needs thousands of quick yes-or-no answers a second from a table of numbers, a small model built for that one job is worth weighing up first.

blocks.title: The old SageMaker tool list
blocks.text: Older guides list SageMaker Data Wrangler, Feature Store and Model Monitor as tools to memorise. The v1.1 guide dropped all three, and Model Monitor is now closed to new customers. You don't need them. Know SageMaker AI as the place you build, train and deploy your own models, with JumpStart as its shelf of ready-made ones.

blocks.label: Now the other three requests
blocks.question: Marketing wants first drafts of product descriptions. There are no data scientists, and the credit union wants the LEAST effort. Which option fits?

options.text: Train a custom text model from scratch in Amazon SageMaker AI
options.why: Cooking from scratch to make one sandwich. Training a writing model needs data, skills and time the credit union doesn't have.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
options.why: Comprehend reads text and tells you about it, like its sentiment. It doesn't write new text.

options.text: A foundation model through Amazon Bedrock
options.why: Right. Writing drafts is exactly what foundation models are good at, and Bedrock gives access through a managed API with nothing to train.

options.text: Kiro
options.why: Kiro is for writing software: specs, code, docs and tests. Marketing copy isn't a software project.

verdict.headline: C. Rent the generalist for general jobs
verdict.body: Nobody needs to explain to a regulator why a product description used the word "flexible". Low stakes, creative output and least effort point at a foundation model through Bedrock. The same logic sends the developers to Kiro and the finance director to Amazon Quick. Only the loans needed a model built for one job.
verdict.aside: If you picked Comprehend, it's the classic mix-up between reading text and writing it. Episode 5's verbs apply: Comprehend understands, it doesn't create.
