blocks.question: The foundation model writes Tom's product descriptions in fluent English. But what does it actually read?
body: Not letters. Not words, either. Before your prompt reaches the model, it gets chopped into pieces and turned into long lists of numbers.
And somehow those numbers know that "loan" and "mortgage" are close relatives, while "loan" and "lawn" are strangers. Next time: how text becomes numbers that know what they mean.

episodes.title: The model never sees a word
episodes.deck: Tokens, embeddings, vectors, transformers. How text becomes numbers that know what they mean.

items.q: Put these circles in order, biggest first: deep learning, AI, generative AI, machine learning.
items.a: AI, then machine learning, then deep learning, then generative AI. Each one sits inside the one before it. Generative AI is a kind of deep learning, which is a kind of ML, which is a kind of AI.

items.q: A model is being fed a huge pile of past examples so it can learn patterns. Is that training or inferencing?
items.a: Training. Inferencing is the later part, when the finished model gets a new input and gives you an answer.

items.q: Your pile of customer emails has no tags on it at all. Nobody has marked which ones are complaints. Which kind of learning can still work on it?
items.a: Unsupervised learning. It finds groups and patterns in unlabelled data. Supervised learning needs the right answer attached to every example.

paras: A customer types “couch” into an online furniture shop's search box. The shop sells 400 couches. The search returns nothing.
Every product page says “sofa”. The old search matched letters, and c-o-u-c-h shares no letters in the right order with s-o-f-a. To the software, they were as different as “couch” and “carburettor”.
The new AI assistant on the same site gets it right first time. Yet it has never read the word “couch” either. It never reads any word at all.
It sees numbers. And somehow the numbers for “couch” and “sofa” sit almost on top of each other.
You run customer support for an online furniture shop. It's Monday, and your queue has 30 tickets that all say roughly the same thing: “Your site says you have no couches. Are you closing down?”
You check. The shop has 400 couches in stock. You type “couch” into the search box yourself. Nothing.
The product team explains over chat. The search matches letters. Every listing says “sofa”, so “couch” finds nothing. They'd need to add every synonym by hand, for every product, forever.
Then someone tries the new AI shopping assistant the company has been testing. “Show me a grey couch for a small flat.” It returns six grey sofas, the smallest first.
Nobody taught it that couch means sofa. It never saw either word as letters. How did it know?

panels.sub: The shop has 400 of them in stock.

panels.line: Every listing says “sofa”.

panels.line: “Grey couch, small flat” → six grey sofas.
It never read either word.

lab.setup: A shop's search matches letters. A shopper types “couch”. Every product is listed as “sofa”, so the search finds nothing. An AI assistant on the same site finds the sofas straight away.
lab.task: Before reading on, write one sentence on what the assistant must be comparing, if it isn't comparing letters. Check it against the steps below.

blocks.text: A model can only do maths, so text has to become numbers before anything else happens. The first step is cutting the text into tokens. AWS defines a token as a sequence of characters that a model treats as a single unit of meaning. A token can be a whole word, a piece of a word like “-ed”, a punctuation mark like “?”, or a common phrase like “a lot”. Think of fridge-magnet poetry. You don't get every word in English, just a box of pieces you can stick together to make any word.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: A language model is given the word “unbelievably”. What does it actually take in?

options.text: The whole word, looked up in a giant dictionary
options.why: A dictionary would fail on every typo, new slang word and product name. Models get round that by working with pieces instead.

options.text: One or more tokens: pieces of the word, each turned into numbers
options.why: Right. Common words may be a single token. Longer or rarer ones get split into pieces, and each piece becomes numbers.

options.text: Each letter, one at a time
options.why: Tokens can be single characters, but going letter by letter makes the text very long and throws away the meaning in common chunks like “un-” and “-ly”.

options.text: A picture of the word
options.why: Some models can take images, but a text model doesn't photograph your words. It cuts them into tokens.

verdict.headline: B. Tokens are the model's alphabet
verdict.body: Every piece of text going into a model, and every piece coming out, is counted in tokens. That's also how you'll be billed later in the course. The exam asks what a token is, and the answer is always a unit of text the model handles as one piece, not a word and not a letter.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, that's how most people imagine it. Now you'll remember that the model has never looked up a word in its life.

blocks.title: From “grey couch” to six sofas
blocks.intro: Here's what happens between the shopper typing and the assistant answering. Watch where the meaning appears.

steps.d: “Show me a grey couch” becomes a short list of tokens. AWS calls this tokenization: breaking text into smaller units, which can be words, parts of words or characters.

steps.t: 2. Turn each token into a vector
steps.d: A vector is a list of numbers that places something in a space with many directions. Picture a map with hundreds of directions instead of just north and east. Each token gets a position on it.

An embedding is the vector that represents a word, sentence, picture or product. AWS says embeddings exist so you can compare how similar different things are. Things that mean similar things end up close together. “Couch” and “sofa” land next to each other, and “carburettor” lands far away.

steps.t: 4. The transformer reads the tokens in context
steps.d: A transformer is the neural network design behind today's large language models. It was introduced in 2017. Its trick is self-attention: every token looks at the other tokens around it to work out what it means here. “Bank” next to “river” and “bank” next to “loan” come out different.

steps.t: 5. The model produces the next token
steps.d: The answer is generated one token at a time. Each new token is chosen from the most likely candidates, given everything so far. Then the tokens are turned back into text for you to read.
It never matched letters. It compared positions, and “couch” sat right beside “sofa”.

blocks.text: Two more words from the same toolkit. Chunking is cutting a long document into small pieces so it fits in the model's context window, which is how much text the model can consider at one time. A 300-page manual won't fit in one go, so you chunk it first. Chunking works on whole documents. Tokenizing works on the text inside them.

Now the model families. A foundation model is a very large model with a huge number of parameters, trained on a massive amount of varied data, so it can be used for many different jobs. Parameters are the numbers the model learned, including its embeddings. A large language model (LLM) is one class of foundation model: the text kind, usually a transformer. A multimodal model takes more than one type of input. Amazon Nova Pro, for example, takes text, images, video, documents and code. A diffusion model makes images differently. It starts from a random sample and changes it in small, controlled steps until a picture appears. It's like a photo slowly coming into focus, one pass at a time.

blocks.title: How a transformer works inside
blocks.text: AWS describes transformers as an encoder and a decoder with self-attention, and its articles also mention GANs and VAEs. None of that is tested as engineering. Know what each term in the objective is for and which job it matches. Nobody will ask you to draw an attention layer.

blocks.label: Match the model to the job
blocks.question: A design agency wants a model that turns a text description into a brand-new image. It starts from random noise and refines the picture step by step. Which kind of model is being described?

options.text: A diffusion model
options.why: Yes. Starting from randomness and improving it in controlled steps is exactly how AWS describes diffusion models.

options.text: An embedding model
options.why: Embedding models turn things into vectors so you can compare them. They measure similarity. They don't paint pictures.

options.text: A text-only large language model
options.why: An LLM generates text one token at a time. The hint words “random noise” and “refines the picture” point elsewhere.

options.text: A classification model
options.why: Classification sorts inputs into labels, like spam or not spam. It picks from options you already have and never creates new content.

verdict.headline: A. Noise, refined in steps, means diffusion
verdict.body: The exam loves describing how a model works and asking you to name it. “Noise” and “step by step” mean diffusion. “Compare similarity” and “semantic search” mean embeddings. “Text and images in the same prompt” means multimodal. “Predicts the next token” means an LLM.
verdict.aside: If you picked C, remember that plenty of image tools take a text prompt. The prompt is only the input. The noise-to-picture process is what makes it diffusion.

blocks.intro: Questions here describe what something does and ask for its name, or give a business need and ask which idea fits. Spot the hint words.

rows.tag: “smallest unit of text the model processes”, “counted for billing”
rows.text: Token.

rows.tag: “numerical representation”, “semantic similarity”, “find items with similar meaning”
rows.text: Embeddings, stored as vectors.

rows.tag: “split long documents to fit the context window”
rows.text: Chunking.

rows.tag: “accepts text, images and video in one request”
rows.text: Multimodal model.

rows.tag: “iteratively refines random noise into an image”
rows.text: Diffusion model.

rows.tag: Trap: “an embedding is a way to compress or encrypt text”
rows.text: Wrong. An embedding stores meaning as numbers so things can be compared. It isn't a zip file, and it isn't security.

rows.tag: Trap: “tokens and words are the same thing”
rows.text: Wrong. One word can be several tokens, and a token can be a punctuation mark or a short phrase.

rows.tag: Trap: “every foundation model is an LLM”
rows.text: Wrong. LLMs are one class of foundation model. Image and multimodal models are foundation models too.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Tokens are pieces of text. Embeddings are meanings as positions. Close together means similar.

blocks.question: If the model only ever picks the next likely token, what stops it picking a likely one that's false?
body: Look again at step 5. The model chooses what sounds most likely next. Nothing in those steps checks whether it's true.
In 2023, two New York lawyers found this out in front of a federal judge. The cases they cited had names, judges and quotes. None of them existed.

episodes.deck: Hallucination, nondeterminism, and the jobs generative AI is actually good at.

items.q: A shopper searches “couch” and the AI finds products listed as “sofa”. What was it comparing?
items.a: Embeddings. Each piece of text becomes a vector, a list of numbers that marks its position by meaning. “Couch” and “sofa” sit close together, so they match.

items.q: How does a large language model produce an answer: all at once, or piece by piece?
items.a: Piece by piece. It generates one token at a time, each chosen from the most likely candidates given everything before it.

items.q: A fraud model flagged 100 transactions and 90 were really fraud. Which metric is that, precision or recall?
items.a: Precision. Of the ones it flagged, how many were right. Recall asks the other question: of all the real fraud, how much did it catch.

paras: Roberto Mata said a metal serving cart hit his left knee on an Avianca flight from El Salvador to New York. He sued. The airline asked a federal court in New York to throw the case out.
His lawyers replied with a filing full of earlier court decisions that supported them. One was “Varghese v. China Southern Airlines”. It had a case number, a court, judges and quotes.
Neither the airline's lawyers nor the judge could find it. Five more cited decisions didn't exist either. All six had come from ChatGPT.

One lawyer had even asked ChatGPT, “Is Varghese a real case?” It said the case “does indeed exist”, and could be found on the big legal research databases. In June 2023 the judge fined the firm and two lawyers $5,000, and called one fake opinion's legal analysis “gibberish”.

It's spring 2023. You're a lawyer at a small New York firm. Your client, Roberto Mata, says an airline serving cart struck his knee on a flight to JFK. The airline, Avianca, wants the case dismissed, and you need earlier decisions that back you up.

Your firm mostly works in state courts, and this one is federal. Someone suggests the new chatbot everyone is talking about. You ask it for cases. It gives you them, neatly formatted, with judges' names and quotes.
You try to look one up, “Varghese v. China Southern Airlines”, and can't find the full text. Maybe it's unpublished, you think. You file anyway.

Avianca's lawyers reply that they can't find most of your cases. Neither can the judge. When he orders copies, you go back to the chatbot and ask it straight out: is Varghese a real case? It says the case does indeed exist, and that you'll find it on Westlaw and LexisNexis. Six of your cases were never written by any court.
The judge will later say there's nothing improper about using a reliable AI tool. The problem is that lawyers must check what they file. The fine is $5,000.

“Is Varghese a real case?”

lab.setup: A lawyer asks a chatbot for court decisions that support his client. It returns six, with case numbers and quotes. He asks it whether one is real, and it says yes. None of the six exist.
lab.task: Before reading on, write down which single check would have caught this before the filing went in. Then compare it with the fixes at the end of the steps below.

blocks.text: You met the cause last episode. A language model writes by picking the next likely token, over and over. A court case name followed by a case number and a quote is a very likely shape for legal text. So the model produced that shape. Nothing in the process checks the result against a real list of cases. AWS calls this a hallucination: output that is inconsistent, factually incorrect or unrelated to the prompt. It's autocomplete with a law degree and no library card.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: Why did ChatGPT insist that the fake case “does indeed exist”?

options.text: Its training data included a fake legal database
options.why: There's no sign of that, and it isn't needed. The model can produce a convincing case from the patterns of real ones.

options.text: Someone had tampered with the chatbot
options.why: Nothing was hacked. The same thing happens with a perfectly working model, which is exactly why it's dangerous.

options.text: It generates likely-sounding text, and “yes, it exists” was a likely reply
options.why: Right. Asking the model to check itself just gets more likely-sounding text. It has no built-in fact check to consult.

options.text: It was set to lie when it doesn't know an answer
options.why: Lying needs knowing the truth. The model doesn't know which of its outputs are true. It knows which ones sound right.

verdict.headline: C. Fluent is not the same as true
verdict.body: Hallucination isn't a bug in one chatbot. It comes from how generation works. That's why asking the same model “are you sure?” is not a check. The judge's point was the fix: a human stays responsible for checking the output before it's used.
verdict.aside: If you picked D, you gave the model too much credit. It isn't clever enough to lie, and that makes it harder to catch.

blocks.title: Four ways generative AI lets you down
blocks.intro: The exam lists four disadvantages. Each one has a failure you'd recognise at work.

steps.d: Confident output that's made up. The Mata filing is the famous example. In a shop chatbot, it's a discount the shop never offered.
Wrong or misleading answers, even without inventing anything. The model can also reflect mistakes and biases in the data it learned from.

Ask the same question twice and you can get two different answers. AWS puts this down to the stochastic, or chance-based, nature of generation. Great for fresh marketing copy. Bad when an auditor asks you to reproduce yesterday's decision.
Nobody can point to the reason the model gave an answer. AWS says generative models are often considered black boxes. A regulator asking “why was this customer refused?” gets no good reply.

AWS suggests better prompts, retrieval augmented generation (RAG, which makes the model look up real documents before answering) or a different model. Add a human check for anything that matters. Later episodes cover each one.

blocks.text: None of that makes generative AI useless. The exam names four advantages. Adaptability: one model handles many different tasks. Responsiveness: answers come back in seconds. Conversation: people can ask in plain language and follow up. Content generation: it writes, draws and speaks new material. The use cases in the exam guide follow from that: summarisation, AI assistants, translation, code generation, customer service agents, search, recommendation engines, and image, video and audio generation. Notice the pattern. They're all drafts, first passes and helpers, where a person or a check can catch the mistakes.

blocks.title: Splitting hairs between hallucination and inaccuracy
blocks.text: The exam guide lists hallucinations and inaccuracy as separate disadvantages, and you could spend an evening deciding where one ends. Don't. AWS's own definition of hallucination already includes “factually incorrect”. Questions turn on the hint words: made-up facts, citations or policies point to hallucination, and the fix is grounding plus human review. You won't be asked to rule on the borderline.

blocks.label: Where does it fit?
blocks.question: An insurance company is considering generative AI for four jobs. Which one is the WORST fit for a generative model on its own?

options.text: Summarising long claim-call transcripts for the claims team
options.why: A good fit. Summarisation is a core use case, and a person reads the summary before acting on it.

options.text: Drafting friendly replies to customer emails for agents to edit
options.why: A good fit. Content generation with a human editing every draft before it goes out.

options.text: Approving or refusing claims, where each decision must be repeatable and explained to a regulator
options.why: Right. Nondeterminism breaks “repeatable”, and interpretability breaks “explained”. That calls for fixed rules or a traditional ML model you can explain.

options.text: Translating policy FAQs into Spanish for review by a bilingual editor
options.why: A good fit. Translation is on the exam's list of use cases, and a reviewer checks the result.

verdict.headline: C. Exact, repeatable and explainable is not a GenAI job
verdict.body: When a question stresses the same answer every time, a reason you can show an auditor, or zero tolerance for made-up facts, generative AI alone is the wrong pick. When it stresses drafting, summarising, translating or chatting, with a human or a check behind it, generative AI fits.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you were right to worry about hallucination. But a summary a person reads is a draft. A claim decision is the final word.

blocks.intro: Expect a scenario with a symptom, then a question asking which limitation it shows, or whether generative AI suits the job at all.

rows.tag: “made-up citations”, “confident but false”, “invented a policy”
rows.text: Hallucination.

rows.tag: “different answer to the same prompt each time”
rows.text: Nondeterminism.

rows.tag: “cannot explain how it reached the output”, “black box”
rows.text: Interpretability.

rows.tag: “summarise”, “draft”, “translate”, “answer questions in plain language”
rows.text: Good generative AI use cases.

rows.tag: Trap: “ask the model to confirm its own answer”
rows.text: Wrong. It will confidently confirm a hallucination, as the Varghese case showed. Check against real sources or use human review.

rows.tag: Trap: “hallucinations mean the model was hacked”
rows.text: Wrong. Hallucination comes from normal generation. It happens in a model that's working as designed.

rows.tag: Trap: “GenAI for a decision that must be identical and auditable”
rows.text: Wrong fit. Use rules or a traditional ML model you can explain.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Generative AI drafts. Something real has to check it: documents, rules or a person.

blocks.question: If the model got its habits from the text it was trained on, who chose that text?
body: The model that invented Varghese had read so much real legal writing that it could fake it perfectly. Someone picked that data, trained on it for weeks and decided it was ready.
Almost no company does that part itself. But you need to know every step, because you'll be asked which ones you still own.

episodes.title: How a foundation model gets made
episodes.deck: Data, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, feedback — and which steps you'll never pay for.

items.q: What makes a model a foundation model rather than an ordinary one?
items.a: Size and range. A foundation model has a huge number of parameters and was trained on a massive amount of varied data, so one model can do many different jobs.

items.q: A chatbot gives a customer two different answers to the same question on two days. Which limitation is that?
items.a: Nondeterminism. Generation involves chance, so the same prompt can produce different outputs.

items.q: Your company wants a model but has no data scientists and no appetite for running servers. Managed API service or self-hosted model?
items.a: Managed API service. You send requests and AWS runs the model. A self-hosted model is one your own organisation deploys and manages.

paras: The CFO of a 200-person travel-booking company reads a headline about AI and sends one line to the product team. “Why don't we just build our own model? Then we own it.”

The head of product has to answer by Thursday. She knows one fact already. AWS describes building a foundation model from scratch as needing GPU clusters running non-stop for weeks. Those are the specialist chips models train on.
She also knows the company's real goal. More visitors who chat with the booking assistant should end up buying a trip.
So the honest answer isn't yes or no. It's a list of seven steps, and a line through most of them.
You're the head of product at a travel-booking company with 200 staff. It's Tuesday, 9:40am, and the CFO has sent you a one-line message: “Why don't we just build our own model? Then we own it.”
You open a blank document. You could write “because it's hard”, but the CFO pays for things that pay back, not things that are hard.

You look up what building from scratch involves. AWS's own description is blunt: GPU clusters, the specialist chips models train on, running continuously for weeks. And before that, a massive pile of training data you don't have.
Then you think about what you actually need. A booking assistant that answers in under a second and helps more visitors actually buy.
By lunchtime your document has seven steps on it. You've crossed out two of them. The question is which two.

panels.line: “Why don't we just build our own model?”
GPU clusters, running continuously, for weeks.
panels.sub: Plus a massive pile of data you don't have.

panels.line: An assistant that helps more visitors book.
Seven steps. Two crossed out.
panels.sub: Which two?

lab.setup: A travel company's CFO wants to build its own foundation model. The actual goal is a booking chatbot that helps more visitors buy a trip.
lab.task: Before reading on, list the steps you think it takes to make a foundation model, in order. Cross out any your company could skip by using a ready-made model. Check your list against the steps below.

blocks.text: Every foundation model goes through the same lifecycle. The exam lists seven stages: data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment and feedback. Think of training a new hire. First someone gives them years of general schooling. Then you teach them your company's way of working, check their work, let them loose on customers and listen to the complaints. The schooling is pre-training. Everything after it is the part you might do yourself.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The travel company decides to use a ready-made foundation model. Which lifecycle stage is it almost certain to skip?

options.text: Evaluation
options.why: Never skip this one. Even a borrowed model has to be tested on your own questions before customers see it.

options.text: Pre-training
options.why: Right. The model provider already did the expensive schooling. You start from the finished model.

options.text: Model selection
options.why: This is exactly the step you do more of. Using a ready-made model means choosing between many of them.

options.text: Feedback
options.why: Feedback is how you find out it's going wrong in real use. Skipping it is how chatbots end up in the news.

verdict.headline: B. Pre-training is the step you rent, not run
verdict.body: Pre-training is where the cost lives: weeks of GPU clusters and a massive amount of data. It's done once by the model provider. Most companies select a model, maybe customise it, then evaluate, deploy and collect feedback. When a question says “LEAST cost” or “fastest”, building from scratch is almost never the answer.
verdict.aside: If you picked C, you spotted that picking a model is work. It's the work that replaces pre-training, which is why you'll remember it.

blocks.title: The seven stages, and who usually does each
blocks.intro: Read each stage, then check the last line of each one: provider, or you.

steps.d: Choose what the model will learn from. The data has to be relevant, accurate, consistent and balanced. Unbalanced data leads to biased output. For a brand-new model, the provider does this. If you customise later, you pick your own data.
Choose the model family and size that fit the job. For most companies this is the first real decision. Usually you.
Train on a massive amount of unlabelled data. The model learns language patterns without anyone tagging the examples. AWS says it takes GPU clusters running for weeks. The provider, almost always.
Train the finished model a little more on a smaller, task-specific set of examples, so it fits your domain or job. Optional. You, if you need it.
Test whether it's good enough: accurate, relevant, not toxic, fair, and hard to trick. Both of you. The provider tests the general model, and you test it on your job.
Put it where your app can call it. With a managed service, AWS runs it and you connect to it. You decide, AWS operates.
Collect how it does in real use, such as thumbs up and down, complaints and corrections. Feed that into the next round of improvements. You.

blocks.text: Stage 2 is where most exam questions live. The exam's selection factors are model type, performance requirements, capabilities, constraints, compliance, cost, latency and model complexity. Latency is how long you wait for an answer. AWS's guidance boils down to a trade. Larger models often give more detailed and accurate answers, but they respond more slowly and cost more to run. Smaller models are cheaper and often good enough. The booking assistant has to answer in under a second, thousands of times an hour. Picking the biggest model available is how the CFO's question comes back as a bill.

blocks.title: Parameter counts and model sizes
blocks.text: AWS's decision guide mentions that large models often have more than 50 billion parameters. Don't memorise that, or any model's size. New models arrive every month and the numbers change. The exam asks about the direction of the trade: bigger usually means more capable, slower and more expensive, and smaller usually means faster and cheaper. Know the direction and you can answer any version of the question.

blocks.label: Pick the model
blocks.question: The booking assistant answers simple questions about baggage and dates. It must reply in under a second, at high volume, as cheaply as possible. Which choice fits best?

options.text: The largest, most capable model available
options.why: It would answer well, but slowly and expensively. Simple baggage questions don't need it.

options.text: A smaller, faster model that handles the task well enough
options.why: Right. Low latency and low cost at high volume point to a smaller model, as long as it passes evaluation on your questions.

options.text: Pre-train a new model on the company's booking data
options.why: Weeks of GPU clusters to answer baggage questions. That's the most expensive option on the list, not the cheapest.

options.text: Whichever model tops a public leaderboard this month
options.why: Leaderboards measure general ability. Your constraints are speed, cost and your own questions, and a leaderboard knows none of them.

verdict.headline: B. Fit the model to the constraint
verdict.body: Read the constraint words in the question. “Real-time” or “low latency” pushes you smaller. “Complex reasoning” or “highest quality” pushes you larger. “Cost-effective” pushes smaller again. The best model is the smallest one that passes your evaluation.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, that's the most common mistake in real projects too. Bigger feels safer until the invoice arrives.

blocks.text: Finally, how does the CFO know it worked? Not from the model's accuracy alone. The exam lists business metrics. Conversion rate: out of every 100 visitors who chat, how many book. Average revenue per user (ARPU): what the average customer spends. Customer lifetime value (CLV): what a customer is worth over the whole relationship, not one trip. Efficiency: how much staff time it saves. ROI, return on investment, puts the gain against the cost. If conversion goes from 3 bookings per 100 chats to 4, that's a number a CFO understands.

blocks.intro: Questions describe a lifecycle stage and ask its name, or give constraints and ask which model to choose, or name a goal and ask which metric proves it.

rows.tag: “from scratch”, “massive unlabelled data”, “weeks of compute”
rows.text: Pre-training. The provider's job, and the most expensive stage.

rows.tag: “smaller task-specific dataset to adapt an existing model”
rows.text: Fine-tuning.

rows.tag: “user ratings”, “thumbs down”, “improve over time from real use”
rows.text: Feedback.

rows.tag: “more chat visitors complete a purchase”
rows.text: Conversion rate.

rows.tag: “value of a customer over the whole relationship”
rows.text: Customer lifetime value.

rows.tag: Trap: “choose the largest model for the best results”
rows.text: Wrong when the question stresses latency or cost. Larger is slower and more expensive to run.

rows.tag: Trap: “every company must pre-train its own model”
rows.text: Wrong. Most companies start from a pre-trained foundation model and skip that stage.

rows.tag: Trap: “model accuracy proves the business value”
rows.text: Not on its own. The exam wants a business metric, like conversion rate, ARPU or ROI.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Providers pre-train. You select, customise, evaluate and listen. Pick the smallest model that passes, and prove it with a business metric.

blocks.question: So you skip pre-training and pick a ready-made model. Pick it from where?
body: The travel company doesn't want one provider's model forever. It wants to try three and switch next year without rewriting the app.
And legal has a question of its own. If the prompts include customers' names and trip details, does the model's maker get to read them?

episodes.title: One API, many models
episodes.deck: Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker JumpStart, Nova — and why most exam answers start with Bedrock.

items.q: Which stage of the foundation model lifecycle does almost every company skip, and why?
items.a: Pre-training. It needs a massive amount of data and GPU clusters running for weeks, so the model provider does it once and everyone else starts from the finished model.

items.q: A chatbot must answer in under a second at high volume, cheaply. Bigger model or smaller model?
items.a: Smaller, as long as it passes your evaluation. Larger models are usually more capable but slower and more expensive to run.

items.q: What is Amazon SageMaker AI for?
items.a: Building, training and deploying your own machine learning models. It's the workshop where data scientists make models, rather than a shop where you pick one ready-made.

paras: A hospital group wants a tool that turns long discharge notes into a plain-English summary for patients. The pilot uses a well-known foundation model from an AI company.
The hospital's lawyer reads the plan and writes one line in red. “No patient note may be sent to the model's maker. Full stop.”
The project lead expects that to kill it. Instead, the AWS documentation says the model's maker has no access to the prompts or the answers at all.
The model is the same one. The front door is different.

You're an analyst at a regional hospital group. For three weeks you've been testing a foundation model that rewrites discharge notes into plain English. Nurses love it. Patients finally understand their medication lists.
Then the lawyer reads the plan. She writes one line in red: “No patient note may be sent to the model's maker. Full stop.”
You assume that's the end. Surely using a company's model means sending it your text?

A colleague from the cloud team sends you a link to an AWS page. It says model providers have no access to the accounts where the models run, no access to the logs, and no access to customer prompts or answers.
Same model. Same summaries. You forward the page to the lawyer and wait. What exactly did you just switch to?

lab.setup: A hospital wants to use a well-known AI company's model to summarise patient notes. Its lawyer forbids sending any note to that company.
lab.task: Before reading on, write down how you could use a company's model without that company seeing your data. Then check your idea against the first bet.

blocks.text: The door is Amazon Bedrock. AWS describes it as a fully managed service that gives secure access to high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies, so you can build generative AI apps. Three things make it the default exam answer. It's serverless: AWS's FAQ says you don't manage any infrastructure. It's one API, a single way for your app to send requests, whichever model you pick, so switching models takes minimal code changes. And it offers many providers, including Amazon, Anthropic, DeepSeek, OpenAI and others. Think of a food court. One till, many kitchens, and you never go into the kitchen yourself.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The hospital calls a third-party model through Amazon Bedrock. What happens to the patient notes in its prompts?

options.text: They go to the model's maker, who uses them to improve the model
options.why: This is what the lawyer feared. AWS says the opposite: your content isn't used to improve the base models and isn't shared with any model provider.

options.text: They stay with AWS, stored at rest in the hospital's chosen Region. The model's maker can't see them
options.why: Right. Providers have no access to the Bedrock accounts, the logs or the prompts and answers. Content is stored at rest in the AWS Region you're using.

options.text: They're kept private, but AWS uses them to train Amazon's own models
options.why: No. AWS says inputs and outputs aren't used to train Amazon Nova, Amazon Titan or any third-party model.

options.text: They're safe only if the hospital fine-tunes its own copy first
options.why: Fine-tuning does make a private copy, but you don't need it for privacy. Ordinary requests are already kept away from the provider.

verdict.headline: B. Your prompts aren't the provider's training data
verdict.body: This is the most tested Bedrock fact. Your content isn't used to train the base models and isn't shared with model providers. It's encrypted in transit and at rest, and you can control the encryption keys with AWS KMS, the Key Management Service. Any question that says “data must not be used to train the model” or “must not leave our control” points to Bedrock.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you're thinking of free consumer chatbots, where that worry is fair. Remember the lawyer's red line, and you'll remember the answer.

blocks.title: Four names the exam puts side by side
blocks.intro: They all involve models. They differ in how much of the work you do yourself.

steps.t: Amazon Bedrock: rent a model through one API
steps.d: Serverless, many providers, nothing to run. Try models in the playground, a console screen for testing prompts, then call the same API from your app. The least effort to get generative AI working.

steps.t: Amazon Nova: Amazon's own family of models
steps.d: Nova is a set of foundation models from Amazon. You reach them through Bedrock. Some understand text, images and video. Canvas generates images, Reel generates video and Sonic handles speech. Nova is a model. Bedrock is where you use it.

steps.t: SageMaker JumpStart: a model hub inside SageMaker AI
steps.d: A library of pre-trained, open-source models, algorithms and ready-made solutions. You can train and tune them further before you deploy them yourself. More control than Bedrock, and more to manage.

steps.t: Amazon SageMaker AI: the full workshop
steps.d: Build, train and deploy your own models. For teams with data scientists and a problem no ready-made model solves.
Bedrock, then JumpStart, then SageMaker AI. Each step down gives you more control and more work.

blocks.text: The exam lists the advantages of AWS generative AI services in words you'll see in answer options: accessibility, a lower barrier to entry, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, speed to market, and meeting business objectives. They all mean one thing. You skip pre-training and infrastructure, so a small team ships in weeks. The exam also names benefits of AWS infrastructure. Security and compliance: Bedrock holds certifications such as ISO and SOC, and it's HIPAA eligible for health data. Responsibility: under the shared responsibility model, AWS protects the infrastructure and you control your content and who can reach it. Safety: tools like Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter what goes in and out, covered in a later episode.

blocks.title: The list of models on Bedrock
blocks.text: At the time of writing, AWS says Bedrock offers 100+ foundation models from many providers. New ones arrive nearly every month, and so do new version names. Don't memorise the menu. The exam asks what Bedrock is for: many providers, one API, serverless, and your data kept private. The same goes for Amazon Bedrock PartyRock, a no-code playground you'll see in older study guides. The current exam guide dropped it.

blocks.label: Bedrock or JumpStart?
blocks.question: A research team wants to choose an open-source pre-trained model, tune it further on its own data, and deploy it in SageMaker AI where it controls the setup. Which option fits best?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock
options.why: Bedrock is the answer when the question stresses least effort and no infrastructure. This team wants a model hub and control over deployment.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
options.why: Right. JumpStart is the SageMaker AI hub of pre-trained, open-source models that you can train and tune further before deploying.

options.text: Amazon Nova
options.why: Nova is a family of Amazon models, not a hub for choosing open-source ones. You reach it through Bedrock.

options.text: Amazon Comprehend
options.why: Comprehend is a ready-made text analysis service for jobs like sentiment. You can't pick and tune a foundation model with it.

verdict.headline: B. “Open-source”, “model hub” and “inside SageMaker” mean JumpStart
verdict.body: Both give you ready-made models. Bedrock keeps everything serverless behind one API. JumpStart hands you the model inside SageMaker AI to tune and deploy with more control. Look for “LEAST operational overhead” (Bedrock) against “full control” or “open-source model hub” (JumpStart).
verdict.aside: If you picked A, that's a good instinct for most questions, which is exactly why the exam writes this one. The hint words tell you when it's the exception.

blocks.intro: Expect a company with a goal and a constraint, then four AWS names. Most of these questions have Bedrock in the answer. The skill is spotting the one that doesn't.

rows.tag: “foundation models from multiple providers”, “single API”, “no infrastructure to manage”
rows.text: Amazon Bedrock.

rows.tag: “data not used to train the model”, “not shared with the model provider”
rows.text: Amazon Bedrock's data privacy.

rows.tag: “hub of pre-trained open-source models” in SageMaker AI, “tune before deploying”
rows.text: SageMaker JumpStart.

rows.tag: “Amazon's own foundation models”
rows.text: Amazon Nova, used through Bedrock.

rows.tag: Trap: “Bedrock sends prompts to the model provider for training”
rows.text: Wrong. Providers can't see prompts or answers, and your content doesn't train the base models.

rows.tag: Trap: “use SageMaker AI to build and train a model” when the question says LEAST effort
rows.text: Wrong. That's the most work. Least effort for generative AI is Bedrock.

rows.tag: Trap: “Nova is an alternative to Bedrock”
rows.text: Wrong. Nova is a set of models, and Bedrock is how you reach them.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Least effort, many models, private data: Bedrock. Open-source model you tune and deploy yourself: JumpStart. Your own model from scratch: SageMaker AI.

Your content isn't used to train the base models and isn't shared with model providers. It's stored in your Region.
Amazon's own foundation models, used through Bedrock. Canvas makes images, Reel makes video, Sonic handles speech.
A hub of pre-trained, open-source models and solutions inside SageMaker AI. You can tune them before you deploy.
A console screen in Bedrock where you try prompts on models before writing any code.
AWS protects the infrastructure. You control your content and who can reach it.

blocks.question: Serverless means no servers to pay for. So what does the hospital pay for?
body: The pilot bill arrives. It isn't counted in hours, or in users, or in summaries.
It's counted in tokens, and one line on it grew fast. A nurse had been pasting in the full discharge note, plus a page of instructions, every time.

episodes.title: You pay by the token
episodes.deck: On-demand, provisioned throughput, batch — and why a longer prompt costs real money.

items.q: A model reads the word “unbelievable”. Does it see one word?
items.a: Not necessarily. It sees tokens: small pieces of text such as whole words, parts of words or punctuation. A long word can be several tokens. Keep hold of that, because tokens are also what you get billed for.

items.q: Your legal team asks whether the model provider behind a Bedrock model gets to read your prompts or train on them. What do you tell them?
items.a: No. AWS says your content is not used to improve the base models and is not shared with any model providers. Providers don't have access to your prompts, completions or Bedrock logs.

items.q: A job scores a million records overnight, and nobody looks at the results until morning. Which kind of inference fits: real-time or batch?
items.a: Batch. Real-time is for someone waiting on an answer right now. When nobody is waiting, you send the whole pile at once and collect the results later.

paras: You're the operations analyst at a mid-sized travel company. Six weeks ago the support team launched a chatbot on Amazon Bedrock. Customers love it. Finance does not.
This month's Bedrock bill is three times last month's. The number of customer chats barely moved. The answers are the same length. Nobody switched models.
You dig through the change log and find one line. Two weeks ago someone “improved accuracy” by pasting the full 40-page travel policy into every single prompt, ahead of the customer's question.
The customer asks a question of about 20 words. The bot sends thousands of words with it. Every one of those words has a price.
It's Monday morning at a travel company, and you're the operations analyst. The finance lead is at your desk before your coffee has cooled. She's holding a printout of the AWS bill.
“The chatbot costs three times what it did,” she says. “Did we triple our customers?”
You didn't. You check the dashboard: the same number of chats, and answers of about the same length. The model is the same one you launched with.
Then you open the prompt the bot sends. Before the customer's short question about baggage fees sits the entire 40-page travel policy. It's in every prompt, every time.
Someone added it two weeks ago to make the answers more accurate. It worked. It's also why finance is standing at your desk.

panels.line: The bill tripled.
panels.sub: Same number of chats. Same answers. Same model.

panels.line: “Can I bring a second bag?”
panels.sub: About ten words.

panels.line: The whole 40-page travel policy, then the question.
panels.sub: Every chat. Every time.

panels.line: “Why does a longer question cost more?”
panels.sub: Because the meter counts what goes in, not only what comes out.

lab.setup: A chatbot's monthly bill tripled. Chat volume is flat, answers are the same length, and the model hasn't changed. The only change: every prompt now starts with a 40-page policy document before the customer's question.
lab.task: Before reading on, write down what you think Bedrock charges for: each request, each answer, or something else. Then check your guess against the first bet.

blocks.text: The default way to pay for a model on Amazon Bedrock is on-demand. No setup and no contract: you call the model and pay for what you use. What you use is measured in tokens, the small chunks of text a model reads and writes. The price is set per million tokens, and it varies by model provider, model size and AWS Region. The part people miss is that input tokens and output tokens are counted separately. Input is everything you send: instructions, pasted documents, chat history and the question. Output is what the model writes back. Think of a taxi meter that also runs while you're loading the luggage.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The travel chatbot's bill tripled. Chat volume, answer length and the model all stayed the same. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Only output tokens are billed, so the answers must secretly be longer
options.why: Output is billed, but so is input. The answers didn't change, so this can't explain a bill that tripled.

options.text: Input tokens are billed too, and every prompt now carries the whole policy
options.why: Right. On-demand pricing counts the tokens you send as well as the ones you get back. Forty pages in every prompt means paying for forty pages on every chat.

options.text: Bedrock charges a flat fee per request, and that fee went up
options.why: On-demand pricing isn't per request. It's per token, which is why prompt length matters at all.

options.text: A longer prompt automatically moves you to a bigger, pricier model
options.why: Prompt length doesn't change which model runs. You choose the model, and your requests go to that model.

verdict.headline: B. The meter runs on what you send
verdict.body: Every token in the prompt is billed, whether it's the customer's ten words or a policy manual. Answer length drives output cost. Prompt length drives input cost. When a scenario says “long prompts” or “large documents in every request”, the exam wants you to connect it to higher token cost and often higher latency, since the model has more to read before it answers. Sending only the relevant pages, which is what retrieval does in a later episode, cuts both.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you're thinking of the answer as the product. The prompt is billed too. Your first surprising AWS bill will make you glad you learned it here.

blocks.title: Three ways to pay for the same model
blocks.intro: Bedrock sells the same model three ways. The question is always whether someone is waiting, and how steady the traffic is.

steps.t: On-demand: pay per token as you go
steps.d: No commitment. You're billed per million input and output tokens. It suits traffic that's new, spiky or hard to predict, like a chatbot you launched last week.

steps.t: Batch inference: send the pile, collect later
steps.d: You submit many prompts at once. Bedrock works through them asynchronously, meaning in the background, and writes the responses to an Amazon S3 bucket. For select models it costs 50% less than on-demand. The catch is that nobody gets an instant answer.

steps.t: Provisioned Throughput: reserve capacity at a fixed price
steps.d: Throughput is how many tokens a model can handle per minute. You buy it in Model Units and pay by the hour. Choose no commitment, 1 month or 6 months. The longer the commitment, the lower the hourly price. It suits predictable, high-volume workloads.
Billing continues until you delete it, busy or idle. It's like renting a delivery van by the month: cheap per parcel when it's full, expensive when it sits in the car park.

steps.t: Custom models: a fourth line on the bill
steps.d: If you customise a model, for example by fine-tuning it on your own data, training is billed on the tokens processed, and you pay monthly to store the model. Then, to use it, AWS says you must buy Provisioned Throughput.

blocks.text: Where you run the model changes the bill too. Prices vary by AWS Region, and not every model is offered in every Region. Content Bedrock processes is stored at rest in the Region where you use it, which matters when a regulator says data must stay in one country. Cross-Region inference lets Bedrock route requests to other Regions' capacity when one Region is busy. The geographic kind keeps requests inside an area such as the US or the EU. The global kind can route anywhere and costs about 10% less, but gives up that boundary. AWS adds no routing charge for either. The trade-off in every exam scenario is the same: responsiveness, availability and residency on one side, cost on the other.

blocks.title: Actual prices and the newer service tiers
blocks.text: Don't memorise what any model costs per million tokens. Prices change often and differ by model and Region, and the exam never asks for a number. You'll also see newer options on the pricing page, such as Priority and Flex service tiers. They aren't in the exam guide. Learn the shape instead: on-demand is per token, batch is cheaper but not instant, and Provisioned Throughput is a fixed hourly price for steady volume and custom models.

blocks.label: Now pick the payment plan
blocks.question: An insurer has Bedrock write summaries of 200,000 claim notes every night. Analysts read the summaries the next morning. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: On-demand inference, sending each note as it arrives
options.why: It works, but you pay the full per-token price for speed nobody needs. Nobody reads the summaries until morning.

options.text: Batch inference, submitting the night's notes as one job
options.why: Right. Nobody's waiting, the job is large, and batch costs 50% less than on-demand for select models. The results land in S3 by morning.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment
options.why: Provisioned Throughput bills every hour, including the long stretches when the nightly job isn't running. It suits steady, predictable traffic, not one nightly burst.

options.text: Fine-tune a smaller custom model to do the summaries
options.why: This adds training and storage costs, and a custom model needs Provisioned Throughput to run. It makes the bill bigger, not smaller.

verdict.headline: B. Nobody waiting means batch
verdict.body: Big job, no one waiting, results needed later: that's batch every time. On-demand is for live traffic that's hard to predict. Provisioned Throughput is for steady high volume, or for serving a custom model. The exam hides this in timing words like “overnight”, “next morning” or “no real-time requirement”.

blocks.intro: Cost questions describe the traffic and the deadline, then ask which way of paying fits. Read the timing words first.

rows.tag: “unpredictable traffic”, “just launched”, “pay only for what you use”
rows.text: On-demand inference. Per-token pricing with no commitment.

rows.tag: “large number of prompts”, “results not needed immediately”, “lowest cost”
rows.text: Batch inference. Asynchronous, results written to S3, 50% cheaper for select models.

rows.tag: “consistent high volume”, “guaranteed throughput”, “custom model”
rows.text: Provisioned Throughput. A fixed hourly price, bought in Model Units, with longer terms costing less per hour.

rows.tag: “long prompts”, “entire document in every request”
rows.text: Higher input-token cost and slower answers. Send only the relevant text.

rows.tag: Trap: “Only the model's output is billed”
rows.text: Wrong. Input and output tokens are both billed, and priced separately.

rows.tag: Trap: “Use Provisioned Throughput for a once-a-night job to save money”
rows.text: Wrong. It bills every hour until you delete it, so idle hours cost money. A nightly job is batch.

rows.tag: Trap: “Batch inference for a live customer chatbot”
rows.text: Wrong. Batch is asynchronous. A customer waiting for a reply needs on-demand or provisioned capacity.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Someone waiting and traffic unpredictable: on-demand. Nobody waiting: batch. Steady and heavy, or a custom model: Provisioned Throughput. Every token you send is on the bill.

blocks.question: What happens to the bill when the model stops answering and starts doing?
body: So far every model in this course has done one thing: read a prompt and write an answer. A person then decides what to do with it.

The next kind of system doesn't wait for a person. It reads the request, decides what to do, looks things up, calls other systems and checks its own work, over and over, until the job is done. Every one of those steps is another prompt.

episodes.title: The model that does things
episodes.deck: Agentic AI: tools, memory, MCP, and several agents that hand work to each other.

items.q: A model tells a customer, confidently and in perfect English, about a discount that doesn't exist. What's the name for that?
items.a: A hallucination: output that sounds right but is factually wrong or not based on the input. Fluent isn't the same as true.

items.q: You ask a model the same question twice and get two different answers. Is it broken?
items.a: No. Generative models are nondeterministic: the response can vary each time because the model picks its next word with some randomness.

items.q: In the four circles of AI, ML, deep learning and generative AI, what does agentic AI add?
items.a: Action. Generative AI produces content. Agentic AI uses a model to decide on steps and carry them out towards a goal, instead of only answering.

paras: You're the operations manager at a regional grocery delivery company. Your support chatbot answers “Where's my order?” about 3,000 times a day.
Its answer is always the same polite paragraph: how to find the tracking page, and how to call the depot if the order is late.
The customer already knew that. They wanted someone to look up order 88412, see that the van broke down, and move the delivery to tomorrow.
Your chatbot can write a beautiful paragraph about rescheduling. It can't reschedule anything. The CEO asks the question you've been dreading: “Why can't it just do it?”
It's 6:40pm at a grocery delivery company, and you're the operations manager. A van has broken down on the ring road with 40 orders on it.
The chat queue lights up. Forty customers type some version of “Where's my food?”
The chatbot replies to every one of them with the same helpful paragraph. Check the tracking page. Call the depot if your order is late. Have a lovely evening.
Your two human agents spend the next hour doing what the customers actually wanted. They look up each order, check the van's status, move the slot to tomorrow and issue a voucher.
It's four steps across three systems, and the chatbot could describe every one of them. Your CEO forwards you a screenshot the next morning with one line: “Why can't it just do it?”

panels.line: Forty customers ask: “Where's my food?”
“Please check the tracking page.”
panels.sub: Forty times. Word for word.

panels.line: Look up the order. Check the van. Move the slot. Send a voucher.
panels.sub: Four actions, three systems.

panels.line: “It knows how. Why can't it just do it?”

lab.setup: A chatbot can explain the four steps to reschedule a late grocery order: look up the order, check the van, move the slot, issue a voucher. It can't perform any of them.
lab.task: Before reading on, list what the chatbot would need, beyond a smarter model, to actually do those four steps. Aim for three things.

blocks.text: The chatbot's problem isn't intelligence. It has no hands. An AI agent is a system that can perform tasks on its own and interact with its environment to reach a goal. AWS's Bedrock definition is more mechanical: an application that works through a task by repeatedly interpreting inputs and producing outputs with a foundation model. Picture a capable new hire. A plain chatbot is a new hire with no phone, no logins and no notebook, who can only give advice. An agent is the same person on day thirty, with access to the order system, a notebook of what they've already done, and a plan.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: What turns the grocery chatbot into something that can actually reschedule the order?

options.text: A larger, more capable foundation model
options.why: A bigger model writes a better paragraph about rescheduling. It still can't touch the order system without a way to call it.

options.text: Tools it can call, memory of the task so far, and a loop that plans the next step
options.why: Right. Tools give it hands, memory keeps track of what's done, and the plan-act-check loop keeps going until the goal is met.

options.text: A lower temperature so its answers are more consistent
options.why: That makes the same paragraph more repeatable. Repeatable advice is still advice, not action.

options.text: A longer prompt describing every rescheduling rule
options.why: More rules make its explanation more accurate and its bill bigger. It still has nothing to act with.

verdict.headline: B. An agent is a model plus hands, a notebook and a plan
verdict.body: The model is the brain in the middle. It becomes an agent when it can call tools, remember what's happened, and choose its next step towards a goal. The exam leans on this: when a scenario says “take actions”, “multi-step task” or “interact with other systems”, it's describing an agent, not a better chatbot.
verdict.aside: If you picked A, you've spotted the most common mistake in real projects too. People buy a smarter model when the fix was giving it access.

blocks.title: What's inside an agent
blocks.intro: AWS guidance splits an agent into parts. Watch the new hire assemble.

steps.d: The agent reads what came in: a customer message, an email, an alert. For the grocery agent, it's “Where's order 88412?”

steps.t: Cognition: set a goal and plan
steps.d: The model works out what done looks like and which steps get there. Find the order, check the van, move the slot, send a voucher.

A tool is anything the agent can call to act or fetch information: an order lookup, a calendar, a payments system. AWS says agents extend their capabilities by using specialised tools. This is the part the chatbot was missing.

Short-term memory holds the current task, the conversation so far and recent results, like a sticky note. Long-term memory keeps knowledge from past experience, like a notebook, so the agent can reuse what worked and avoid repeating mistakes.
The agent feeds what happened back in, so the next evening with a broken-down van goes better than the last.
Plan, act, look at the result, plan again, until the goal is met. That repeated cycle is what makes it an agent rather than a single answer.

blocks.text: Every tool needs a connection. If you wire each model to each system by hand, ten agents and ten systems means a hundred custom connections. Model Context Protocol (MCP) fixes that. It's an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic, that connects AI applications to external data sources and tools in one standard way. Think of it as a universal plug: build a socket for your order system once, and any MCP-compatible agent can use it. An MCP server offers three kinds of thing: resources (data to read), tools (actions to take) and prompts (reusable instructions). AWS's line to remember: a single protocol eliminates the need for custom integrations for each AI-to-system connection.

Big jobs get split between agents. A workflow orchestration agent coordinates multistep tasks across systems and delegates work to subagents, much like a shift lead handing jobs to specialists. AWS names two multi-agent patterns. Vertical is a hierarchy: a supervisor agent sends work down to specialist agents and gathers the results. Horizontal is lateral collaboration: specialist agents work side by side as peers and pass work to each other. Real businesses already run this way. AWS describes customer service agents that find answers across a company's systems, take action, and escalate to a human when they can't.

blocks.title: Amazon Bedrock Agents
blocks.text: Older courses teach Amazon Bedrock Agents in detail: action groups, knowledge bases, configuration screens. The v1.1 exam guide dropped it, and AWS has renamed it Bedrock Agents Classic, closed to new customers from July 30, 2026. AWS now points people to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore instead, which is next episode. If an old practice question's answer is “Bedrock Agents”, the question is out of date.

blocks.label: Now the one the exam asks
blocks.question: A company has five AI agents that each need to read from the same internal inventory system. It wants to connect them without building five separate custom integrations. What should it use?

options.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP), exposing the inventory system once for any compatible agent
options.why: Right. MCP is the standard plug. Build one MCP server for the inventory system, and every compatible agent can call it.

options.text: Fine-tune each agent's model on a copy of the inventory data
options.why: Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves, not what it can connect to. The data would also be stale the moment stock changes.

options.text: Long-term memory, so each agent remembers the inventory
options.why: Memory stores what an agent has learned or done. It isn't a live connection to a system of record.

options.text: A vertical multi-agent pattern with one supervisor agent
options.why: That decides who hands work to whom. It doesn't solve how any agent reaches the inventory system.

verdict.headline: A. One protocol, no custom wiring
verdict.body: Whenever a question pairs agents with “external systems”, “tools” or “data sources” and adds “standard” or “without custom integrations”, the answer is MCP. Memory is what the agent remembers. Orchestration is who does what. MCP is how it reaches the outside world.

blocks.intro: Agent questions describe what the system has to do, then offer you the pieces. Match the need to the part.

rows.tag: “perform multi-step tasks”, “take actions”, “interact with other systems”
rows.text: An AI agent: a foundation model with tools, memory and a loop.

rows.tag: “connect agents to external data sources and tools”, “standard protocol”
rows.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP). Primitives: resources, tools, prompts.

rows.tag: “remember the conversation so far” vs “recall past interactions across sessions”
rows.text: Short-term memory vs long-term memory.

rows.tag: “supervisor agent delegates to specialist agents”
rows.text: Vertical (hierarchical) multi-agent pattern, run by a workflow orchestration agent.

rows.tag: “specialist agents collaborate as peers”
rows.text: Horizontal multi-agent pattern.

rows.tag: Trap: “Use a larger model so the chatbot can take actions”
rows.text: Wrong. Size improves answers, not reach. Actions need tools.

rows.tag: Trap: “MCP is an AWS service you turn on in the console”
rows.text: Wrong. MCP is an open protocol, a standard, introduced by Anthropic. AWS services support it, but it isn't a product.

rows.tag: Trap: “Amazon Bedrock Agents” as the modern answer
rows.text: Out of date. Dropped from v1.1 and closed to new customers. AgentCore is the current AWS platform.

rows.tag: Rule
rows.text: Agent = model + tools + memory + a loop. MCP is how it plugs into systems. Orchestration is how several agents share the work.

blocks.question: So where does the grocery agent actually run?
body: You now know what an agent is made of. Your developer knows how to write one. Your security lead has one question: when this thing logs into the order system at 6:40pm, whose permission is it using, and who can see what it did?
AWS has a separate answer for building the agent, running it, writing its code and handing it to business users. They have four different names, and the exam will offer you all four.

episodes.deck: AgentCore runs them, Strands builds them, Kiro writes the code, Quick answers the business.

items.q: An agent needs to connect to a ticketing system, a calendar and a CRM without custom code for each. What standard does it use?
items.a: Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol that connects AI applications to external tools and data in one standard way.

items.q: What's the difference between an agent's short-term and long-term memory?
items.a: Short-term memory holds the current task and conversation. Long-term memory keeps what the agent learned across sessions, so it can reuse strategies and avoid repeat mistakes.

items.q: A team wants to try foundation models from several providers through one API, with no servers to manage. Which AWS service?
items.a: Amazon Bedrock. It's the fully managed, serverless way to reach many providers' foundation models.

paras: You're three weeks into a job as the AI programme lead at a mid-sized bank. On Monday, five teams send you five requests.

The developers want help turning a feature request into specs, code and tests. The finance analysts want to ask their dashboards questions in plain English. Two engineers want to build an agent in a few lines of code. The platform team wants somewhere safe to run that agent for 10,000 customers. The infrastructure team wants to move old .NET applications onto Linux.
Each request has a different AWS answer. On Friday the architect asks you to name all five out loud.
It's Monday at a mid-sized bank, and you're the new AI programme lead. Your inbox has five messages, all sent before 9am, all marked urgent.

The developers: “We want an AI that turns a feature request into a spec, then code, then tests.” The finance analysts: “We want to ask our dashboards questions in plain English and automate the monthly report.”
Two engineers: “We've written an agent in a few lines of code. Now what?” The platform team: “If that agent goes live for customers, it needs isolation, memory, logins and audit trails.”
The infrastructure team: “Can AI help us move our old .NET apps onto Linux?”
At Friday's review, the architect points at the whiteboard. “Which AWS service for each?” Everyone looks at you.

panels.line: Specs and code. Dashboards. An agent in a few lines.
Run it safely for 10,000 customers. Move old .NET apps to Linux.
“Which AWS service for each?”
They all involve agents.
panels.sub: Only one of them is the place agents run.

lab.setup: Five teams ask for: (1) specs, code and tests from a prompt; (2) plain-English questions over business dashboards; (3) an open-source way to build an agent in a few lines; (4) a secure place to run agents at scale; (5) help moving old .NET apps to Linux.
lab.task: Before reading on, guess which of these five names fits each request: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, Kiro, Amazon Quick, AWS Transform. Check your guesses against the steps below.

blocks.text: All five of these products use agents, which is exactly why the exam can swap them. The trick is to ask who the user is and what they're doing. A developer writing code? A developer building an agent? An operations team running agents? A business analyst? A team moving old systems? One question, five answers. Think of a restaurant: the recipe book, the kitchen, the chef's assistant, the waiter and the removal van that moves you to a new building.

blocks.label: Commit before you read on
blocks.question: The bank's engineers built a customer-support agent with an open-source framework. The platform team now needs to run it for thousands of customers with isolated sessions, memory, and tracing. Which service fits BEST?

options.text: Strands Agents
options.why: Strands is how you write an agent. The agent is already written. The need now is running it in production.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
options.why: Right. Runtime gives isolated sessions, Memory keeps context, and Observability traces what the agent does. It works with any framework and any model.

options.text: Kiro
options.why: Kiro helps developers write code from specs. It isn't where a customer-facing agent runs.

options.text: Amazon Quick
options.why: Quick gives business users AI over their data and tasks. It isn't a hosting platform for your own agents.

verdict.headline: B. Build anywhere, run on AgentCore
verdict.body: The giveaway words are “deploy”, “operate”, “at scale”, “session isolation”, “memory” and “observability”. Those describe running agents, and running agents is AgentCore's job. AgentCore doesn't care which framework built the agent, so “built with LangGraph” or “built with Strands” doesn't change the answer.
verdict.aside: If you picked Strands, you matched the word “agent” to the agent-building SDK. Next time, look for the verb. Building means Strands. Running means AgentCore.

blocks.title: Five names, five jobs
blocks.intro: Each one in AWS's words, then who it's for.

steps.t: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: where agents run
steps.d: AWS calls it an agentic platform for building, deploying and operating agents securely at scale, with any framework and any foundation model. It works with open-source frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex and Strands Agents. It's the kitchen: you bring the recipe, it provides the stoves and the safety rules. Pricing is consumption-based, with no upfront commitment.

steps.t: Inside AgentCore: the parts the exam names
steps.d: Runtime is a secure, serverless place to deploy agents, with each user's session kept isolated. Memory gives short-term memory for a conversation and long-term memory across sessions. Gateway turns your APIs and Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools. Identity manages how agents log in and act on behalf of users. Policy sets deterministic boundaries on what agents may do. Observability lets you trace, debug and monitor agents in production.

steps.t: Strands Agents: how you write an agent
steps.d: An open-source SDK, which is a toolkit of code for developers. AWS says it takes a model-driven approach to building and running AI agents in just a few lines of code. A Strands agent is a model, some tools and a prompt, and it can use thousands of published MCP servers. It's the recipe book.

steps.t: Kiro: the agent that helps you write code
steps.d: An agentic coding service that turns prompts into detailed specs, then into working code, docs and tests. It adds agent hooks and steering files, and it runs on Amazon Bedrock. It's the chef's assistant, for developers building any software.

steps.t: Amazon Quick: AI for the business user
steps.d: An AI-powered service for automating tasks, analysing data, building web apps and doing research. It includes Quick Sight for dashboards and business intelligence, plus Quick Flows, Quick Automate, Quick Index and Quick Research. It connects to other systems through MCP and OpenAPI. It's the waiter: the people ordering never see the kitchen.

steps.t: AWS Transform: agents that modernise old systems
steps.d: A service that uses agentic AI to speed up transforming infrastructure, applications and code. Examples include mainframe applications, VMware servers moved to Amazon EC2, and .NET apps moved to Linux-ready .NET. AWS says there's no additional charge to use it. It's the removal van.

blocks.text: Two of AgentCore's parts come back in the security episode, so learn their shape now. AgentCore Identity lets agents reach AWS resources and outside services on behalf of users, while keeping security controls and audit trails. Policy in AgentCore checks every request an agent makes through AgentCore Gateway against your rules before it reaches a tool. The rules are written in a policy language called Cedar, or in natural language.

blocks.title: AgentCore's newest add-ons
blocks.text: AgentCore's docs also list Code Interpreter, Browser, Evaluations, Harness, Registry, Payments and Optimization. They're real, and more keep arriving. None is in the exam guide. Learn Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, Policy and Observability, and let the rest go. You'll also meet Amazon Q in older material. The exam's service list names Amazon Quick, and AWS now points Amazon Q Business customers to Quick.

blocks.label: Now the business side
blocks.question: The bank's finance analysts don't write code. They want to ask questions of their sales dashboards in plain English, run research and automate a monthly reporting task. Which service should they use?

options.text: Kiro
options.why: Kiro is for people writing software. The analysts want answers and automation, not code.

options.text: Amazon SageMaker AI
options.why: SageMaker AI is for building, training and deploying your own ML models. That's a data scientist's tool, not an analyst's.

options.text: Amazon Quick
options.why: Right. Quick covers data analysis with Quick Sight, research with Quick Research, and task automation with Quick Flows and Quick Automate, all for business users.

items.q: A team needs guaranteed capacity for steady, heavy traffic on one model, at a fixed hourly price. Which Bedrock option?
items.a: Provisioned Throughput. You buy Model Units by the hour, and longer commitments cost less per hour. It's also what you need to serve a custom model.

items.q: Developers want help turning a feature request into specs, code and tests. Analysts want plain-English answers from dashboards. Which service does each group want?
items.a: Developers want Kiro, the agentic coding service. Analysts want Amazon Quick, the AI service for business users.

items.q: Name two things, other than quality, that decide which foundation model a business should pick.
items.a: Any two of: cost, latency, compliance, model type, capabilities, constraints, performance requirements and model complexity. Quality is only one factor on the list.

paras: You're the data analyst at an online furniture retailer. The catalogue team needs 2 million product descriptions sorted into 12 categories: sofas, lamps, rugs and so on.
The engineers pick the most powerful model Bedrock offers. It reads text, images and video, and it can reason through long documents. The results are excellent.
They also take four seconds each, and the test run's bill is more than the catalogue team's quarterly budget.
Meanwhile, the marketing team's tagline tool keeps suggesting “Comfort, redefined.” for every sofa. Every single time. Two teams, one model menu, and both picked wrong.
It's Thursday at an online furniture retailer, and you're the data analyst. Two complaints arrive before lunch.

The first is from the catalogue lead. Her team needs 2 million product descriptions sorted into 12 categories. Engineering chose the biggest multimodal model on the menu, one that reads images and video as well as text. The test run on 10,000 items was flawless, slow and eye-wateringly expensive. Scale that up and it's the whole quarter's budget.
The second is from marketing. Their tagline generator gives the same line for every sofa: “Comfort, redefined.” They've tried asking nicely. It says it again.
Both teams think they need a better model. Neither does.
